sources.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says - CNBC
passages: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.
The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.
Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 .
The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups.
There have also been many quality and production problems, including several recalls.
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.
"Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019.

extraction.body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year. Musk , who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment , said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for production of its Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said. Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 . The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. sources.title: RIP Cybertruck — Elon Musk says production is 'winding down' at its Texas Gigafactory, as Tesla says the pick-up 'lives on through Cybercab' - TechRadar
passages: Elon Musk has used his X account to reveal that Tesla will be "winding down" production of its divisive Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas around "the middle of next year", in order to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi .
Musk stopped short of saying whether this means the end of the Cybertruck altogether, or merely that production is going to be moved elsewhere.
But the project’s lead, Wes Morrill, posted a more reflective statement to the social media site, saying: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab".

One X user wrote: "Serious concern for continuity on Model 3 and Y... sensing here an end on consumer products from Tesla," while another pointed out that the winding down of Cybertruck could mean for owners that they “won't get meaningful software updates anymore” and Cybertruck's software will grow “increasingly stale”.

It is not a nailed-on fact that Cybertruck is dead, but it is a good indicator that Tesla is considering wiping yet another EV from its line-up… a worrying trend that points towards a growing focus on autonomous vehicles and its Cybercab program .

From claiming it had over one million reservations for the truck shortly after it launched in 2023, to estimations placing deliveries at around 30,000 for all of 2026 — way down on the planed 250,000 annual sales — it hasn’t shipped in the numbers Tesla predicted.
Tesla also massively over-promised and under-delivered.

It failed to deliver its range-extending battery pack, which was supposed to offer the claimed electric mileage the company originally boasted, while its much-lauded Cybertent, or Basecamp, was a $3,000 disappointment.

Elon Musk has used his X account to reveal that Tesla will be "winding down" production of its divisive Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas around "the middle of next year", in order to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi . Musk stopped short of saying whether this means the end of the Cybertruck altogether, or merely that production is going to be moved elsewhere. But the project’s lead, Wes Morrill, posted a more reflective statement to the social media site, saying: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab". That sounds a bit like an obituary to us and many users rushed to post their responses, which ranged from high praise for the angular electric pick-up truck, calming it was “the best vehicle ever made” to blunt putdowns. Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production November 6, 2026 Although others highlighted a point that many Tesla commentators have been focussing on in the past few years: the fact that Tesla doesn’t seem all that interested in EVs any more. One X user wrote: "Serious concern for continuity on Model 3 and Y... sensing here an end on consumer products from Tesla," while another pointed out that the winding down of Cybertruck could mean for owners that they “won't get meaningful software updates anymore” and Cybertruck's software will grow “increasingly stale”. Whatever the stance, it is difficult to get away from the fact that Cybertruck has been a commercial disappointment . From claiming it had over one million reservations for the truck shortly after it launched in 2023, to estimations placing deliveries at around 30,000 for all of 2026 — way down on the planed 250,000 annual sales — it hasn’t shipped in the numbers Tesla predicted. Customers have also had to put up with plenty of compromise, including reports of poor off-road performance , disappointing electric range and worries about recalls, one of which was issued over fears that the wheels could fall off . Tesla also massively over-promised and under-delivered. It failed to deliver its range-extending battery pack, which was supposed to offer the claimed electric mileage the company originally boasted, while its much-lauded Cybertent, or Basecamp, was a $3,000 disappointment. Even reducing the price didn't work, as it scrapped the cheapest Cybertruck after just five months on sale. Things haven't been great for Cybertruck ever since chief designer Franz von Holzhausen attempted to demo its "armor glass", only to smash it in front of a live audience. But one of the most obvious signs of its recent demise is the fact that Tesla has made it deliberately difficult to determine just how many it was selling in recent years. The company has been bundling sales figures in with the now-defunct Model S and Model X, as well as the Tesla Semi truck, in order to make the numbers seem more impressive than they actually are. It is not a nailed-on fact that Cybertruck is dead, but it is a good indicator that Tesla is considering wiping yet another EV from its line-up… a worrying trend that points towards a growing focus on autonomous vehicles and its Cybercab program . Aside from the attention-grabbing Roadster, which used flying stunts to make headlines, there has been no talk of real EV innovation, no word on a new model to rejuvenate the current line-up and no attempt to keep up with the sort of battery-swapping, megawatt charging EV infrastructure China is busy introducing to the world. Say what you like about Cybertruck, it has always served as a halo product, something that diverted attention towards the brand. But in automotive circles, halo models only work if showrooms are full of great cars customers actually want to buy. Where Tesla is concerned, that line-up is shrinking and compared to the competition , is rapidly falling behind. coreStoryFacts.text: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.
The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.
Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 .
The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups.
There have also been many quality and production problems, including several recalls.
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.
"Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019.

Elon Musk has used his X account to reveal that Tesla will be "winding down" production of its divisive Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas around "the middle of next year", in order to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi .
Musk stopped short of saying whether this means the end of the Cybertruck altogether, or merely that production is going to be moved elsewhere.
But the project’s lead, Wes Morrill, posted a more reflective statement to the social media site, saying: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab".

One X user wrote: "Serious concern for continuity on Model 3 and Y... sensing here an end on consumer products from Tesla," while another pointed out that the winding down of Cybertruck could mean for owners that they “won't get meaningful software updates anymore” and Cybertruck's software will grow “increasingly stale”.

It is not a nailed-on fact that Cybertruck is dead, but it is a good indicator that Tesla is considering wiping yet another EV from its line-up… a worrying trend that points towards a growing focus on autonomous vehicles and its Cybercab program .

From claiming it had over one million reservations for the truck shortly after it launched in 2023, to estimations placing deliveries at around 30,000 for all of 2026 — way down on the planed 250,000 annual sales — it hasn’t shipped in the numbers Tesla predicted.
Tesla also massively over-promised and under-delivered.

It failed to deliver its range-extending battery pack, which was supposed to offer the claimed electric mileage the company originally boasted, while its much-lauded Cybertent, or Basecamp, was a $3,000 disappointment.

The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.
"Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019.

sources.title: Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
passages: In an X post on Friday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the company will be “winding down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory sometime around the middle of next year, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” The production plant in Austin, Texas, is the only Tesla facility that’s known to assemble the Cybertruck, and that’s equipped to make the specialized components required to build the vehicles.
If the Cybertruck does meet its demise in 2027, Tesla still has another ridiculous vehicle on the horizon to serve as its spiritual successor.

While Tesla doesn’t break out individual Cybertruck sales figures, even the highest analyst estimates place the total number of deliveries at roughly 70,000 since its launch in 2023 — significantly below the 250,000 that Musk once predicted would be sold annually.

extraction.body: Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI). The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms. In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower. Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%. Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value. "The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added. "The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off." Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology. They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday. Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents. "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday. "Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats." "The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social. On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring". Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms. OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board. "A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California. extraction.body: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry. A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March. The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading. Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%. Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe . “Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.” On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%. Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility. The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%. “It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’” Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come. “Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.” However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak. The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July. Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”. He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.” Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March. Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week. Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

extraction.body: Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI). The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms. In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower. Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%. Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value. Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday. The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high. However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year. The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls. The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%. European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback". "The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added. "The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off." Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology. They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday. These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper? Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents. "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday. "Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats." "The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social. On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring". Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms. OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board. "A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California. extraction.body: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry. A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March. The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading. Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%. Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe . “Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.” On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%. Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility. The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%. “It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’” Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come. “Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.” However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak. The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July. Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”. He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.” Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March. Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week. Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

extraction.body: Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI). The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms. In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower. Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%. Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value. Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday. The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high. However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year. The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls. The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%. European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback". "The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added. "The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off." Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology. They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday. Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents. "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday. "Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats." "The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social. On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring". Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms. OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board. "A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California. Changes in the FTSE 100 and other indexes are not just for financial experts, they can affect our lives. Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months. Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its AI own search summaries were affecting ad revenue. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is 355 pages and full of never before disclosed company information. The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. passages: Is there any bigger hype man in mobile tech these days than Nothing CEO Carl Pei?

Pei is easily one of the most visible founders around, regularly starring in videos and posting to social media, responding to creators and just being a whole lot more present in the eyes of consumers than many of his peers.
Now he’s using one of those platforms to tease his company’s “first AI-native product” — and it could be here sooner than you’d think.
According to Pei, Nothing will release an AI-native device sometime in December.
While details are incredibly scant for the moment, he does offer a few tidbits:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission.

Pei suggests that Nothing’s in a prime position to help test these AI-consumer-hardware waters, leaning especially on his firm’s commitment to design, which can easily go overlooked in a tech-first hardware launch.

Over on X, Pei has published a bit of a think piece about the evolution of consumer technology, looking at how first the personal computer, and then the mobile revolution were led by business adoption, before trickling down to the masses.
With AI, he thinks we’re still in that first phase, and the “killer device” that will define the true arrival of the AI hardware era is still taking shape in minds of engineers.
And while that’s still probably years off, Nothing’s not wasting any time getting a head start.
Nothing has reportedly been planning a major shift towards AI-first launches , with wearables and audio hardware rumored to be the company’s new priorities.

sources.title: Nothing to launch its first AI-native product in December; Carl Pei says device will not have a screen
passages: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4.
For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product.
Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI.

Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence.
The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows.
It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.
However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy.
The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware.

extraction.body: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4. The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows. Pei said the product is being built as a dedicated tool rather than an application, although he did not reveal its name, design, pricing or specific features. “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote. The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware. The company has been discussing its plans to build AI-native devices and an operating system designed around artificial intelligence. The teaser offers little information about the device’s form factor. However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy. Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence. “The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life. According to Pei, the adoption of AI will follow a trajectory similar to that of personal computers and smartphones, where workplace applications helped drive initial adoption before the technology became part of everyday consumer life. He argued that personal computers first became useful through tools such as spreadsheets and word processors, while smartphones gained traction through practical applications before becoming central to entertainment and communication. “Product-market fit for AI will come in productivity first, in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today,” Pei wrote. While AI models have become increasingly capable, they often lack access to the information and context needed to perform tasks effectively. He said that even when users connect their inboxes, calendars and messaging platforms to AI agents, important information from everyday interactions can still be missed. “Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. Close it, and everything AI can already do gets dramatically more useful.” Pei believes the next generation of AI tools will need to move beyond chat interfaces and become more proactive. Tomorrow, it will work for you,” he said, arguing that AI could eventually change how individuals collaborate with each other, how organisations interact with people and how humans work alongside intelligent agents. For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product. The company has not yet disclosed whether the device will be a wearable, an audio product or another category of hardware. Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI. The upcoming product will be its first concrete offering under that strategy. The launch also comes amid growing interest in dedicated AI hardware. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices. However, Pei cautioned against expecting one device to immediately transform the AI industry. “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote. Nothing is expected to share more details about its first AI-native product ahead of its December launch.

Pei is easily one of the most visible founders around, regularly starring in videos and posting to social media, responding to creators and just being a whole lot more present in the eyes of consumers than many of his peers. Now he’s using one of those platforms to tease his company’s “first AI-native product” — and it could be here sooner than you’d think. Over on X, Pei has published a bit of a think piece about the evolution of consumer technology, looking at how first the personal computer, and then the mobile revolution were led by business adoption, before trickling down to the masses. With AI, he thinks we’re still in that first phase, and the “killer device” that will define the true arrival of the AI hardware era is still taking shape in minds of engineers. And while that’s still probably years off, Nothing’s not wasting any time getting a head start. According to Pei, Nothing will release an AI-native device sometime in December. While details are incredibly scant for the moment, he does offer a few tidbits: There’s a lot in there that’s quite interesting, considering as little as it actually says. Why qualify that no-screen comment with “new” — will this work with one of the existing screens in your life? And that “couldn’t be an app” claim feels almost proactively defensive. It’s hard to read without thinking about past AI products like that Rabbit R1 device that ended up feeling like just an app in an expensive box . Pei suggests that Nothing’s in a prime position to help test these AI-consumer-hardware waters, leaning especially on his firm’s commitment to design, which can easily go overlooked in a tech-first hardware launch. Finally, he shares the teaser pic you see above, showing us… a very handsome, nearly featureless corner. There’s a hint of a leather-like texture, but that’s about all we can make out from this. So, what is this actually going to be? Nothing has reportedly been planning a major shift towards AI-first launches , with wearables and audio hardware rumored to be the company’s new priorities. Pei mentions a context problem for AI, where we sometimes have great, fleeting ideas that we never take the time to share with an AI model, and so never manage to fully develop them. That sure feels like the sort of issue a recorder or note-taking hardware could assist with. That’s maybe the closest thing to a hint here, but this is also a hardware class that’s kind of been done to death already, with even Amazon getting in on the action . Right now, your guess may be as good as ours. Sound off in the comments for what you think this is likely to be — or maybe share you fears for what you really hope it isn’t. Either way, we should be getting answers in just a few more weeks.

passages: The New York Times Company has reportedly “entered exclusive negotiations” to acquire Letterboxd for $330 million, according to a report from The New York Times itself.
Letterboxd is free, but users can access advanced features with a paid subscription.
Its projected earnings for this year are estimated at $15 million, which is only about 4.5% of what the Times is supposedly offering to buy the company for.
Personally, we wouldn’t be surprised if these anonymous tips were coming from inside the house, so we’re inclined to take this report pretty seriously.

Letterboxd reported 3 million users in January 2021, a figure that grew to 28 million by April of this year.
Letterboxd was previously reported to be seeking a new owner.
According to the Times, film studios A24 and Sony were interested in the acquisition, but A24 was priced out.

Letterboxd, like the Times, earns revenue from both subscriptions and advertising.
The Times Company would integrate its advertising technology with Letterboxd’s systems, two sources said and Letterboxd would most likely continue as a stand-alone site for the foreseeable future.

extraction.body: The New York Times Company is reportedly in exclusive negotiations to acquire the popular movie-oriented social platform Letterboxd for an estimated $330 million. This news has emerged from a report in The New York Times itself, signaling a potentially significant expansion for the media organization into the entertainment space. Letterboxd has experienced remarkable growth in recent years, emerging as a beloved platform for film enthusiasts who wish to catalog and review films, akin to the way Goodreads serves book lovers. The platform boasted 3 million users in January 2021, and that number surged to an impressive 28 million by April 2023. Notably, more than half of Letterboxd’s user base is under the age of 35, highlighting its appeal among younger audiences. The acquisition interest comes after Letterboxd had previously signaled that it was seeking a new owner. While there were reports of interest from film studios like A24 and Sony, A24 reportedly found the acquisition price too steep and withdrew from the bidding process, potentially leaving the field open for The New York Times Company. Currently, Letterboxd operates on a free model with optional paid subscriptions that provide users with advanced features. For 2023, the platform is projected to earn around $15 million, which is only a fraction—approximately 4.5%—of the proposed acquisition price. This discrepancy raises questions about the valuation and future potential of the platform. While The New York Times Company has refrained from commenting publicly on the negotiations, the nature of the source and the paper's own coverage of the story have led to speculation about the credibility of the report. Observers note the irony and intrigue of a news organization reporting on its own potential acquisition, and some suggest that information leaks may be emanating from within the Times itself. As this acquisition could mark a transformative moment for both The New York Times and Letterboxd, industry watchers will be keenly observing how the negotiations unfold and what it might mean for the future of media and entertainment convergence.

extraction.body: The New York Times Company is reportedly in exclusive negotiations to acquire the popular movie-oriented social platform Letterboxd for an estimated $330 million. This news has emerged from a report in The New York Times itself, signaling a potentially significant expansion for the media organization into the entertainment space. Letterboxd has experienced remarkable growth in recent years, emerging as a beloved platform for film enthusiasts who wish to catalog and review films, akin to the way Goodreads serves book lovers. The platform boasted 3 million users in January 2021, and that number surged to an impressive 28 million by April 2023. Notably, more than half of Letterboxd’s user base is under the age of 35, highlighting its appeal among younger audiences. The acquisition interest comes after Letterboxd had previously signaled that it was seeking a new owner. While there were reports of interest from film studios like A24 and Sony, A24 reportedly found the acquisition price too steep and withdrew from the bidding process, potentially leaving the field open for The New York Times Company. Currently, Letterboxd operates on a free model with optional paid subscriptions that provide users with advanced features. For 2023, the platform is projected to earn around $15 million, which is only a fraction—approximately 4.5%—of the proposed acquisition price. This discrepancy raises questions about the valuation and future potential of the platform. While The New York Times Company has refrained from commenting publicly on the negotiations, the nature of the source and the paper's own coverage of the story have led to speculation about the credibility of the report. Observers note the irony and intrigue of a news organization reporting on its own potential acquisition, and some suggest that information leaks may be emanating from within the Times itself. This news has emerged from a report in The New York Times itself, signaling a potentially significant expansion for the media organization into the entertainment space.
Letterboxd has experienced remarkable growth in recent years, emerging as a beloved platform for film enthusiasts who wish to catalog and review films, akin to the way Goodreads serves book lovers.
The platform boasted 3 million users in January 2021, and that number surged to an impressive 28 million by April 2023.
Notably, more than half of Letterboxd’s user base is under the age of 35, highlighting its appeal among younger audiences.
The acquisition interest comes after Letterboxd had previously signaled that it was seeking a new owner.

While there were reports of interest from film studios like A24 and Sony, A24 reportedly found the acquisition price too steep and withdrew from the bidding process, potentially leaving the field open for The New York Times Company.
Currently, Letterboxd operates on a free model with optional paid subscriptions that provide users with advanced features.
For 2023, the platform is projected to earn around $15 million, which is only a fraction—approximately 4.5%—of the proposed acquisition price.
This discrepancy raises questions about the valuation and future potential of the platform.

While The New York Times Company has refrained from commenting publicly on the negotiations, the nature of the source and the paper's own coverage of the story have led to speculation about the credibility of the report.
Observers note the irony and intrigue of a news organization reporting on its own potential acquisition, and some suggest that information leaks may be emanating from within the Times itself.

extraction.body: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more. When was the last time you got a new phone? For me, it was last week. Before that, it might have been three weeks ago. Before that, well, you get the idea — I have some of the best Android phones from the last few years floating around my apartment. In some cases, I have multiple generations of the same lineup, like Google Pixel devices back to the Pixel 6 series and iPhones back to the iPhone 12, and I’ve used them all. It’s a fortunate position to be in, but also one that shows how little tends to change from one year to the next. As someone whose SIM is always on the move, here’s how often I think you should get a new phone. First and foremost, you don’t need a new phone every year. I certainly wouldn’t get one that often if I weren’t in my position. If I’ve learned one thing from my constant stream of new phones, the more they claim to change, the more they tend to stay the same. Apple, Google, and Samsung can mention everything new over the course of an hour-long keynote address, but by the time we get the latest device in hand, it feels so similar to the previous generation. Having reviewed them all, the iPhone 16 feels a lot like the iPhone 14 and 15 did before it, and other than minimizing their camera cutouts, the last few generations of Galaxy S flagships have all felt — and looked — identical. That said, sometimes a significant change will come along that makes you wonder if it’s time to update. Sometimes it is. Apple ushered in its Dynamic Island on the iPhone 14 Pro series, and Google debuted its Tensor chip and revamped camera bar on the Pixel 6 series, both of which felt like steps away from established designs. The Pixel 6 Pro remains the last phone I bought with my own money, and I remember being so excited to see Google finally break free from an endless stream of single-color devices and corner-mounted camera bumps. It was finally an innovation that brought more of the Pixel process in-house and started a leadup to longer software support and a more seamless Pixel experience. Since then, things have slowed down — and not just for the Pixel. The Tensor chip has improved in its G2, G3, and G4 generations, and Google has swapped a few other bits of its Pixel design, but none of it — at least from a hardware perspective — has added up to make some people ready to spend $1,000 on a new phone. Google’s chipset still runs warm at times, its older devices are perfectly capable of image processing, and it’s still tough to top some of the original Pixel 6 color options, even though I think I bought mine in Stormy Black anyway. To an extent, even foldable phones have been lured into a cycle of minor updates. Both Samsung and Motorola adopted larger cover displays for their flip phones in 2023 (which they then kept in 2024), but before that, the Galaxy Z Flip and Razr were starting to feel like rinse-and-repeat launches. They had similar cameras and almost the same hinges for a few years, and choosing to update would cost you a cool $1,000 for a phone that might not last its entire update cycle. And then, 2025 happened. Both Samsung and Motorola decided to give their flagship flip phones a heap of love, with the former finally expanding its Flex Window on the Galaxy Z Flip 7 and introducing a slightly more affordable Fan Edition model, and the latter debuting the no-holds-barred Razr Ultra . The two brand-new flip phones finally feel like exactly what we’ve been looking for when we’ve exercised patience and caution before buying a new phone. Mentioning updates, that’s probably the main reason I’d tell someone to buy a new phone right now. Not for the current state of Android or iOS itself — they haven’t changed much in a few years — but for the fact that you can finally expect more than three or four years of continued updates. After all, if you spend the money on a Pro-level iPhone or anything with Ultra in the name, it’s better to know that you have seven years of support ahead of you rather than half of that. Yet, even with an improved update timeline, I find myself willing to recommend previous-generation flagships more and more as I write reviews. They tend to pack similar cameras and carry comparable displays, and they can often be had at a much more comfortable price. Sure, you’ve probably already missed out on a year of updates, but they’ll be available when you set up your phone, and the money you can save is more than worth your while. There is, however, one thing that might have you eyeing up an upgrade — AI. Now, on-device AI isn’t a must-have feature just yet, but given its strict hardware requirements, it will probably push you into a new phone sooner rather than later. Google has reserved most of its Gemini Nano experience for the Pixel 8 and Pixel 9 series, Samsung’s Galaxy AI is only fully available on the traditional Galaxy S and foldable Galaxy Z lineups, and Apple Intelligence has finally arrived on the iPhone 15 Pro duo and iPhone 16 series. But, as I said, on-device AI isn’t as important as a reliable set of cameras or a vibrant, smooth display — at least not yet. Instead, it feels like Google’s first crack at an in-house chipset — flawed, but a step in the right direction. Where we couldn’t trust the original Tensor to stay cool under pressure, we can’t always trust the accuracy of generative AI features as they land. Generated wallpapers are still full of wonky artifacts, and text often feels robotic and artificial, but both have come a long way in their relatively short histories. They just still have a way to go. Don’t get me wrong, there are some AI-powered features that I’ve started to embrace. Circle to Search is a noticeable improvement on Google Lens, and Magic Editor is a logical step beyond Magic Eraser, but other features like Google’s Magic Compose feel slightly sillier. I can count on zero hands the number of times I’ve wanted to rephrase a text message to sound like Shakespeare before sending it to a friend. To put it another way, AI on smartphones currently feels like the early generations of foldable phones. Sure, it does some neat tricks, and it’ll certainly catch the eye of your nerdier friends, but it’s not quite ready for everyone. Honestly, foldable phones still aren’t ready for everyone, given their lower durability and smaller batteries, and they’ve had generations to iron out the kinks — er, creases. Honestly, I have AI-capable devices in the Pixel 9 Pro and Galaxy S25 Ultra, but I don’t find myself using them any differently from my standard iPhone 15. Now, for the potentially more than $1,000 question — when should you update your phone? Well, the simple answer would be when it stops working. If something happens to it that will cost more to fix than the phone is worth, like a shattered display or a busted battery, it’s time to upgrade. If you’ve run out of Android (or iOS) updates and security patches, it’s time to upgrade. Otherwise, you might want to take a long, hard look at your current phone before you relegate it to the great tech cloud above (or sell it to someone else). When you decide to upgrade, you’ll probably have an all-new slate of the best camera phones and some of the most powerful hardware to choose from. Since phones are guaranteed additional years of updates, are slightly easier to repair, and — let’s face it — have reached something of a plateau, there’s less reason to run out for the latest iPhone or Pixel. Who will tease you for not having the latest and greatest phone when it looks almost the same as its predecessor from two or three years ago? I’d rather have money in my pocket and a phone that does everything I need than the street cred associated with whipping out the Samsung Galaxy Z Scroll Super Max Ultra (this isn’t an actual phone, but it might have made Unpacked more exciting). And yes, I know that telling you not to buy a new phone goes directly against what I do for a living. I know that I should be pressing you to upgrade your phone using one of our affiliate links so that we can get some money and keep the lights on (which would be nice). But I also know that phones and accessories like cases and earbuds are extremely expensive. Life is expensive, too. Unless you can write 1,500 words — approximately the length of this piece — on why a new phone would make your life better than your current, still-supported phone, you can probably wait a little longer.

sources.title: I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
passages: I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself.

It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables.
When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small.

And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo.
And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones.
Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem.
This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option.
These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day.
It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly.
The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo.

extraction.body: When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small. Apps that feel comfortable on Samsung’s short foldable and the similarly sized Xiaomi 18 Fold are often cramped and compact on the Duo’s cover screen, robbed of screen space by a right-hand rail that most apps don’t make use of anyway. That’s just one of the ways that Apple’s first foldable feels fundamentally different from the Android alternatives. I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself. For now at least, Android is slicker for folding phones — though I don’t know how long that will last. Size, shape, and build quality The iPhone Duo feels great. Its curved frame and Ceramic Shield back have that ineffable Apple feeling, a sense of polish that helps justify the $2,000 price tag. At first it feels encouraging, the reassuring heft of all that glass and metal. It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly. The Duo is even shorter and wider than the Z Fold 8, though almost identical in dimensions to Xiaomi’s 18 Fold. I’m a fan of this design, which is both cute and comfortable when folded shut and gives you a natural choice of portrait or landscape orientations when open. The major downsides are that the short cover screen makes some apps awkward to use, and it’s wide when you need to stretch across to the other side — a problem worsened by some of Apple’s software choices. And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo. It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables. It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration. The crease and screen The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones. The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s. Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem. I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here. Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen. This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option. I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan. Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility. They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too. Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall. I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use. It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display. Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down. The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo. Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger. At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space. And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones. Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic. These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day. The bottom line Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws. If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them.

It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration.
The crease and screen The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones.
The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s.
Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem.
I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here.
Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen.
This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option.
I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan.
Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility.
They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too.

Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall.
I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use.
It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display.
Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down.
The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo.
Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger.

At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space.
And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones.

Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic.
These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day.
The bottom line Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws.
If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them.
