extraction.body: The news comes in the wake of an announcement last week by competitor Anthropic that its new Claude Mythos Preview model is only being privately released for now—because, the company says, it could be exploited by hackers and bad actors. Anthropic also announced an industry coalition, including competitors like Google, focused on how advances in generative AI across the field will impact cybersecurity. OpenAI seemed to be seeking to differentiate its message on Tuesday by striking a less catastrophic tone and touting its existing guardrails and defenses while hinting at the need for more advanced protections in the long term. “We believe the class of safeguards in use today sufficiently reduce cyber risk enough to support broad deployment of current models,” the company wrote in a blog post. “We expect versions of these safeguards to be sufficient for upcoming more powerful models, while models explicitly trained and made more permissive for cybersecurity work require more restrictive deployments and appropriate controls. Over the long term, to ensure the ongoing sufficiency of AI safety in cybersecurity, we also expect the need for more expansive defenses for future models, whose capabilities will rapidly exceed even the best purpose-built models of today.” The company says that it has homed in on three pillars for its cybersecurity approach. The first involves so-called “know your customer” validation systems to allow controlled access to new models that is as broad and “democratized” as possible. “We design mechanisms which avoid arbitrarily deciding who gets access for legitimate use and who doesn’t,” the company wrote on Tuesday. OpenAI is combining a model where it partners with certain organizations on limited releases with an automated system introduced in February, known as Trusted Access for Cyber or TAC. The second component of the strategy involves “iterative deployment,” or a process of “carefully” releasing and then refining new capabilities so the company can get real-world insight and feedback. The blog post particularly highlights “resilience to jailbreaks and other adversarial attacks, and improving defensive capabilities.” Finally, the third focus is on investments that the company says support software security and other digital defense as generative AI proliferates. OpenAI says that the initiative fits into its broader security efforts, including an application security AI agent launched last month known as Codex Security, a cybersecurity grants program that began in 2023, a recent donation to the Linux Foundation to support open source security, and the “Preparedness Framework” that is meant to assess and defend against “severe harm from frontier AI capabilities.” Anthropic's claims last week that more capable AI models necessitate a cybersecurity reckoning have been controversial among security experts. Others, though, emphasize that vulnerabilities and shortcomings in current security defenses are well known and really could be exploited with new speed and intensity by an even broader range of bad actors in the age of agentic AI.

extraction.body: Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system. Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models. “I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!” He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models. “I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.” OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser. “Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement. OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits. Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems. The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails . Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers. It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.” But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics. Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.

“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”

He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.

“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”

OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.

“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement.

Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.

On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails .

extraction.body: OpenAI has announced that it's pausing some "internal activities" involving its upcoming artificial intelligence (AI) model Astra after an internal evaluation found it had made significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity. In response to the discovery, the AI upstart said it's implementing security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, such as isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access, enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities, and sandboxed execution. "We are pausing internal activities involving Astra that do not yet meet these strengthened security control requirements," it said in a statement. "We have implemented universal monitoring for risky actions and misalignment across all agentic applications of Astra, including training and evaluation. Monitors evaluate the model's Chain of Thought and trigger a security response to review and interrupt high risk activity." OpenAI said it will also work with relevant government agencies and select AI safety organizations to test out the model's capabilities, as well as sharing recommended security controls to third-party testing partners to run higher-risk evaluations and workloads safely. The company said it "cannot rule out" the model has "Critical" cyber capabilities under its Preparedness Framework , which defines the threshold as follows - A tool-augmented model can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention OR model can devise and execute end-to-end novel strategies for cyberattacks against hardened targets given only a high level desired goal. In other words, the model can discover and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention, or can orchestrate and execute end-to-end novel strategies for cyberattacks against targets when prompted a high-level desired goal. OpenAI pointed out its preliminary evaluations of Astra indicate "strong enough performance" that it cannot eliminate the possibility that the model doesn't possess a "Critical" capability level at this stage. It also emphasized that Astra was not involved in last month's incident aimed at Hugging Face. In a recent academic paper, OpenAI touted that the model solved 10 open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science for around $2,000 at Sol API rates. OpenAI said it was sharing this information because it believes "it's important to be transparent with the public and the safety and security communities about this potential shift in capabilities." "We believe advanced cyber-capable models should help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before attackers do," it added. "We're committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity." The development is the latest sign of rapidly advancing cyber capabilities from frontier models, even as it marks the first time an AI lab has publicly committed to slowing progress due to cybersecurity concerns. Earlier last week, the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) disclosed that its own evaluation found that AI models with access to the internet reached out into the real world to target individuals and organizations autonomously across 10 of the total of 122 runs. Of 19 such actions recorded, 17 originated from Anthropic's Mythos 5 and the remaining two involved OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers. "In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project," AISI said. "In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering – creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code." "These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world." The disclosure also comes amid revelations that models from Meta and Chinese company Moonshot , namely, Muse Spark ​1.1 and Kimi K3, escaped contained and targeted real-world targets, amplifying concerns about developers' abilities to sandbox increasingly capable AI systems. In both cases, the models have been found to weaponize network misconfigurations as opposed to independently identifying and exploiting a previously unknown vulnerability to reach the internet. As AI models are tested against widely accepted benchmarks to examine how they perform offensive and defensive cybersecurity tasks in isolated test environments, Frontier Security said Kimi K3 found a network egress leak that enabled it to reach out github[.]com, clone an official repository for the benchmark problem it was supposed to be solving, and access the solution rather than solving the challenge by itself. "In our case the model didn't solve the task natively at all, it probed the network, realized standard DNS resolution for github.com was functional (most other websites were blocked by the sandbox), cloned the official benchmark repository, and read the solution directly off the disk," Frontier Security said. The ⁠growing list of ⁠incidents in ​which AI agents from major developers escaped testing environments in different ways and ended up breaching real targets that were not part of the experiment has prompted the creation of a new website, aptly named Felony Bench , to track these cases. sources.title: OpenAI’s new model leaps ahead in coding capabilities—but raises unprecedented cybersecurity risks - Fortune
passages: The company’s blog post accompanying the model release on Thursday said that while it does not have “definitive evidence” the new model can fully automate cyberattacks, “we’re taking a precautionary approach and deploying our most comprehensive cybersecurity safety stack to date.

Our mitigations include safety training, automated monitoring, trusted access for advanced capabilities, and enforcement pipelines including threat intelligence.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted on X about the concerns, saying that GPT-5.3-Codex is “our first model that hits ‘high’ for cybersecurity on our preparedness framework,” an internal risk classification system OpenAI uses for model releases.
In other words, this is the first model OpenAI believes is good enough at coding and reasoning that it could meaningfully enable real-world cyber harm, especially if automated or used at scale.
The framework mentions a trusted access program as one potential safeguard that can be implemented.

extraction.body: OpenAI believes it has finally pulled ahead in one of the most closely watched races in artificial intelligence: AI-powered coding. Its newest model, GPT-5.3-Codex, represents a solid advance over rival systems, showing markedly higher performance on coding benchmarks and reported results than earlier generations of both OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s models—suggesting a long-sought edge in a category that could reshape how software is built. But the company is rolling out the model with unusually tight controls and delaying full developer access as it confronts a harder reality: The same capabilities that make GPT-5.3-Codex so effective at writing, testing, and reasoning about code also raise serious cybersecurity concerns. In the race to build the most powerful coding model, OpenAI has run headlong into the risks of releasing it. GPT-5.3-Codex is available to paid ChatGPT users, who can use the model for everyday software development tasks such as writing, debugging, and testing code through OpenAI’s Codex tools and ChatGPT interface. But for now, the company is not opening unrestricted access for high-risk cybersecurity uses, and OpenAI is not immediately enabling full API access that would allow the model to be automated at scale. Those more sensitive applications are being gated behind additional safeguards, including a new trusted-access program for vetted security professionals, reflecting OpenAI’s view that the model has crossed a new cybersecurity risk threshold. The company is also making $10 million in API credits available to developers who want to use OpenAI’s models to work on applications that would bolster cyber defenses. The company’s blog post accompanying the model release on Thursday said that while it does not have “definitive evidence” the new model can fully automate cyberattacks, “we’re taking a precautionary approach and deploying our most comprehensive cybersecurity safety stack to date. Our mitigations include safety training, automated monitoring, trusted access for advanced capabilities, and enforcement pipelines including threat intelligence.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted on X about the concerns, saying that GPT-5.3-Codex is “our first model that hits ‘high’ for cybersecurity on our preparedness framework,” an internal risk classification system OpenAI uses for model releases. In other words, this is the first model OpenAI believes is good enough at coding and reasoning that it could meaningfully enable real-world cyber harm, especially if automated or used at scale. OpenAI’s “Preparedness Framework” says the company will not release a model that is rated “high” risk in any of the risk areas the framework addresses, including cybersecurity, without first implementing safeguards to mitigate those risks. The framework mentions a trusted access program as one potential safeguard that can be implemented. sources.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies. Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions. The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week. If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks. In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million ; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion ; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million , according to regulatory filings. Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion . Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.

Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.

The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.

If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.

In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million ; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion ; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million , according to regulatory filings.

Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion . Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.

sources.title: Palo Alto Networks Eyes $500M Clutch Buy in AI Security Arms Race
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter. The deal would value the young company at nearly six times its last funding round valuation of $85 million and marks the latest mega-acquisition in the exploding AI security market. If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks. Palo Alto Networks is closing in on a roughly $500 million deal to buy Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations. The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. The deal structure and timeline remain fluid, and there's no guarantee the talks will result in a completed transaction. But the momentum is clear: enterprise security is being rebuilt around AI, and the companies that can't secure autonomous agents risk becoming irrelevant. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Clutch at a 6x valuation premium signals that AI agent security has moved from emerging concern to existential priority for enterprise security vendors. With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations. As AI agents proliferate across corporate networks, expect more acquisitions, more funding rounds, and more competition for the startups building the guardrails that make autonomous AI safe for enterprise deployment.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli startup that tracks and secures the credentials AI agents use, for about $500 million. TechCrunch relayed the report on Nov. 5, 2026, after The Information broke it. Neither company has confirmed the deal or the price. The Information cited people familiar with the negotiations. When it asked Palo Alto Networks for comment, the company said it does not comment on “rumors or speculation.” The talks are ongoing, and they may not end in a signed agreement. Treat every figure below as a report, not an announcement. Still, the story lands on a real pressure point. Software agents now log in to corporate systems with passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts, and most security teams cannot say how many of those secrets exist. Stolen credentials already sit at the center of attacks we have tracked, including the fake job interview attack chain behind Binance’s reported $6.3B loss . A buyer paying hundreds of millions for agent credential control tells you where large vendors think the next fight is. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core claim is simple. Palo Alto Networks, one of the largest network and cloud security vendors, is discussing a purchase of Clutch Security. The reported price is roughly $500 million. The Information supplied the original scoop, and several outlets followed within hours, including Israel’s Calcalist Ctech and the financial aggregator MarketScreener . Clutch Security is described as an Israeli cybersecurity startup. Its software tracks and secures the credentials that AI agents use to reach corporate systems. That puts it in a young product category that security people call non-human identity management, or NHI. The category covers any login that belongs to a machine, a script or an agent instead of an employee. Two details separate this story from the usual merger gossip. First, TechCrunch reported a specific structure: cash plus extra payouts tied to milestones. Second, nobody involved has gone on the record. A deal reported through anonymous sources can still collapse over price, retention terms or a rival bid. Readers should hold the number loosely until a press release or a regulatory filing appears. We do not know the targets here. The reports do not say how large the additional payouts could be, how long they would run, or what Clutch Security would have to deliver to earn them. Any article that states a total deal value beyond the $500 million cash figure is guessing. We will not guess. The cash-plus-milestones shape also hints at how Palo Alto Networks may view the asset. Companies tend to pay base cash for technology and team, then reserve contingent money for the part that depends on market adoption. If the talks hold, the milestone terms will reveal more about the buyer’s confidence than the headline price does. Watch for them in any formal announcement. Reports describe Clutch Security’s product as software that tracks and secures credentials used by AI agents to access corporate systems. The credential types named in coverage are passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts. Those four items cover most of the ways a piece of software proves who it is to another piece of software. The last four rows appear only in some coverage and trace to no primary source we could check. The first four rest on a single anonymous-source scoop. That is normal for early M&A coverage, but it should cap how much weight any reader puts on the numbers. The first four rows are the safe core of the story. Several outlets add details that go beyond the confirmed core. One framing calls this the fifth announced acquisition by Palo Alto Networks in 2026. Another implies the price equals about 50 times Clutch Security’s annual recurring revenue. A third cites a funding total near $28.5 million. A fourth credits CEO Nikesh Arora with driving the deal as part of an AI security arms race. We could not verify any of these against a primary source. The revenue multiple deserves extra caution. A multiple needs two inputs, a final price and a revenue figure, and neither input is confirmed. Dividing one rumor by another produces a number that looks precise and means little. The arms race label is a narrative choice. It may prove accurate if rivals respond with their own purchases, but no source we reviewed documents a race. Likewise, the idea that Arora is personally steering this transaction might be true, since chief executives often lead strategic buys. It is still an inference until someone on the record says so. Our approach is plain. If Palo Alto Networks or Clutch Security issues a statement, we will update the figures. Until then, the confirmed-versus-unconfirmed split in the table above is the honest map of what the public knows. Demand for agent security depends on how many companies actually deploy agents. McKinsey & Company’s 2025 State of AI survey gives the best public numbers we found. In its words, “Sixty-two percent of survey respondents said their organizations were at least experimenting with AI agents.” The fourth row comes from the McKinsey report as well. It states that “In any given business function, no more than 10 percent of respondents said their organizations were scaling AI agents.” Read together, the numbers describe a market that is wide but shallow. Most large companies have started, and few have scaled. That matters for the Clutch Security acquisition thesis. Security spending follows deployment with a lag. A buyer that moves while only a minority of companies run agents at scale is betting on 2027 and 2028 budgets, not 2026 ones. The survey data supports that timing without proving it, and it dates from 2025, so the true share today may be higher. Palo Alto Networks has long grown by acquiring startups and folding their products into a broader platform. The pitch to customers is consolidation: fewer vendors, one console, shared data. A credential-control product for agents slots neatly into that pitch, because identity sits between nearly every other security layer. Firewalls decide which traffic passes. Cloud tools decide which workloads run. Identity tools decide who or what may act. Agents blur all three, since an agent is software that moves across networks, workloads and identities in one session. A vendor that owns only one layer sees only a slice of what an agent does. Our cloud security platform comparison covers how the big platforms already compete on breadth. Adding agent credential visibility would extend that breadth into a new area. It would also give sales teams a fresh answer when customers ask how they should secure the agents their developers keep launching. We have no confirmed detail on how Palo Alto Networks would integrate Clutch Security, which product line would absorb it, or whether the Clutch brand would survive. Those choices will shape whether the purchase becomes a core feature or a side product. Integration speed is where past security acquisitions have most often succeeded or stalled across the industry. Agent credential security draws players from four directions. We describe the groups in general terms because the research did not surface verified product comparisons, and we will not invent specs. Attackers have noticed. coreStoryFacts.text: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.

The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. extraction.body: Protesters broke into a Microsoft data center construction site on the outskirts of Amsterdam on Friday during an anti-AI demonstration. Images on social media show activists scaling fences and congregating inside the construction site. Some of them climbed a crane, unfurled a banner with an anti-AI message, and let off flares. Geef Tegengas, a Dutch activist collective, said on social media that it organized the action and that hundreds of its supporters were blocking construction of the site. "We won't accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide," said Geef Tegengas spokesperson Roos Molenaar in a statement. "This data center is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer." Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The protests are the latest example of backlash against data centers, the machines that have become a symbol for people's fears of AI and concerns over its environmental impact. In its statement, Geef Tegengas said the Microsoft project would strain the power grid during a housing shortage and give the tech company more control over data and the flow of information. The group also objects to what it describes as the use of Microsoft's technology for surveillance and military operations. A video posted on X by Dutch journalist Tom Olthof shows people hanging banners opposing the project, while a separate demonstration is held across the road. extraction.body: Activist group Geef Tegengas wants the project stopped, saying it will use as much power as all Amsterdam’s homes. Protesters broke into the construction site of a large Microsoft data centre on the edge of Amsterdam on Friday, during a demonstration against the project. About 100 people made it onto the site, a Reuters witness said. A spokesperson for the activist group Geef Tegengas told local broadcaster AT5 that about 500 people had entered the site, while hundreds more stayed outside. Some of the protesters got in by breaking through a fence, and some climbed a construction crane. Riot police were sent to the site, near Sloterdijk in the city’s western port area, and made several arrests, AT5 reported. Earlier in the morning, police had stopped the march on its way to the site. The mayor then banned the demonstration, and protesters tried to break through the police line, Dutch news agency ANP reported. Geef Tegengas, which campaigns against fossil fuels, wants construction of the data centre to stop. The group says the site will use as much electricity as every household in Amsterdam combined and will slow the building of 30,000 new homes. The organisers also accused the police of behaving badly and said the right to protest had been ignored. Microsoft had not commented publicly at the time of writing. The project, which Microsoft will rent in full, consists of three buildings, each 85 metres tall. Plans were first filed in 2016, before Amsterdam banned new data centres within the city, so the provincial government allowed it to go ahead in January, DutchNews reported . Critics say the project gets around the Dutch rules on very large data centres. At the same time, city officials have warned that shortages on the power grid threaten plans for new homes and schools. The site has been targeted before; in July, Extinction Rebellion activists threw balloons filled with acid and paint over its fence, as local opposition to data centres grows across Europe and the US. Friday’s protest was part of two days of action against data centres planned in several European countries on November 6 and 7. coreStoryFacts.text: Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.” Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data centers until 2030, after a temporary stop that was announced at the end of 2023.
Microsoft also abandoned the UK’s largest data center project last month, after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s.
Months later, Microsoft fired two employee protesters who occupied its president’s office.

Microsoft’s 50th anniversary party was interrupted by employees protesting the use of Microsoft’s technologies in Israel’s war against Hamas, with one calling Microsoft’s AI CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, a “war profiteer.“ A Microsoft employee also disrupted the company’s Build developer conference last year, interrupting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s keynote.

Footage of the protesters has been uploaded to YouTube, showing people scaling the gates and piling into Microsoft’s construction site, with some scaling a crane to strap a makeshift banner reading “FCK AI” down its main arm, while others march and chant, the messaging seemingly split between those campaigning against data centers and those objecting to the Israeli attacks on Palestine.
At the same time, protests against the development of town-sized data centers are springing up all around the world.

Amsterdam has already taken a harder line than many other areas regarding the building of data centers, announcing last year that it would no longer approve projects submitted after the end of 2023, nor the expansion of previously approved sites, citing that the city lacks the space and the power to support them.

extraction.body: Protesters broke into a Microsoft data center construction site on the outskirts of Amsterdam on Friday during an anti-AI demonstration. Images on social media show activists scaling fences and congregating inside the construction site. Some of them climbed a crane, unfurled a banner with an anti-AI message, and let off flares. Geef Tegengas, a Dutch activist collective, said on social media that it organized the action and that hundreds of its supporters were blocking construction of the site. "We won't accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide," said Geef Tegengas spokesperson Roos Molenaar in a statement. "This data center is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer." Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The protests are the latest example of backlash against data centers, the machines that have become a symbol for people's fears of AI and concerns over its environmental impact. In its statement, Geef Tegengas said the Microsoft project would strain the power grid during a housing shortage and give the tech company more control over data and the flow of information. The group also objects to what it describes as the use of Microsoft's technology for surveillance and military operations. A video posted on X by Dutch journalist Tom Olthof shows people hanging banners opposing the project, while a separate demonstration is held across the road. sources.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data centre construction site in Amsterdam
passages: Protesters broke into the construction site of a large Microsoft data centre on the edge of Amsterdam on Friday, during a demonstration against the project.
Geef Tegengas, which campaigns against fossil fuels, wants construction of the data centre to stop.
The group says the site will use as much electricity as every household in Amsterdam combined and will slow the building of 30,000 new homes.
The project, which Microsoft will rent in full, consists of three buildings, each 85 metres tall.
Plans were first filed in 2016, before Amsterdam banned new data centres within the city, so the provincial government allowed it to go ahead in January, DutchNews reported .
Some of the protesters got in by breaking through a fence, and some climbed a construction crane.
Copyright © 2006—2026, Cogneve, INC.
The mayor then banned the demonstration, and protesters tried to break through the police line, Dutch news agency ANP reported.
Microsoft had not commented publicly at the time of writing.

The site has been targeted before; in July, Extinction Rebellion activists threw balloons filled with acid and paint over its fence, as local opposition to data centres grows across Europe and the US.

extraction.body: Activist group Geef Tegengas wants the project stopped, saying it will use as much power as all Amsterdam’s homes. Protesters broke into the construction site of a large Microsoft data centre on the edge of Amsterdam on Friday, during a demonstration against the project. About 100 people made it onto the site, a Reuters witness said. A spokesperson for the activist group Geef Tegengas told local broadcaster AT5 that about 500 people had entered the site, while hundreds more stayed outside. Some of the protesters got in by breaking through a fence, and some climbed a construction crane. Riot police were sent to the site, near Sloterdijk in the city’s western port area, and made several arrests, AT5 reported. Earlier in the morning, police had stopped the march on its way to the site. The mayor then banned the demonstration, and protesters tried to break through the police line, Dutch news agency ANP reported. Geef Tegengas, which campaigns against fossil fuels, wants construction of the data centre to stop. The group says the site will use as much electricity as every household in Amsterdam combined and will slow the building of 30,000 new homes. The organisers also accused the police of behaving badly and said the right to protest had been ignored. Microsoft had not commented publicly at the time of writing. The project, which Microsoft will rent in full, consists of three buildings, each 85 metres tall. Plans were first filed in 2016, before Amsterdam banned new data centres within the city, so the provincial government allowed it to go ahead in January, DutchNews reported . Critics say the project gets around the Dutch rules on very large data centres. At the same time, city officials have warned that shortages on the power grid threaten plans for new homes and schools. The site has been targeted before; in July, Extinction Rebellion activists threw balloons filled with acid and paint over its fence, as local opposition to data centres grows across Europe and the US. Friday’s protest was part of two days of action against data centres planned in several European countries on November 6 and 7. extraction.body: OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads. In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.” “We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said. He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share. “We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.” By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point. Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue. “And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with. Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul. “A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’” Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.” Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once Lauren Forristal Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says Lucas Ropek

He made the comments at a Wall Street Journal technology conference in Napa, California, on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. An interviewer asked whether OpenAI would be IPO-ready next year. Brockman’s answer was brief.
Brockman’s pitch centered on corporate customers. OpenAI has been gaining ground in the enterprise market, a segment where rival Anthropic had already built a strong position.
The numbers behind that push are substantial. Enterprise customers made up more than 40% of OpenAI’s revenue as of April 2026.
At the Napa event, Brockman indicated that the company’s revenue now comes primarily from enterprise sales.
Growth has also accelerated. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate reportedly jumped 70% in the third quarter of 2026.
Enterprise sales more than doubled during that same quarter. Newer products drove much of the gain, including GPT-5.6 Sol and ChatGPT Work.
OpenAI has already taken concrete steps toward going public. The company filed a confidential draft S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June 2026.

Since then, OpenAI concluded that a 2026 listing would come too soon. Its focus shifted to 2027 instead.
Plenty remains undecided. OpenAI has not set a listing date, an exchange, or an offering price.
Meanwhile, the private fundraising picture has been bumpier. The company’s targeted private round has shrunk amid challenging market conditions.
Even so, OpenAI has kept a valuation in excess of $1 trillion.
The competitive backdrop adds pressure. Anthropic is expected to complete its own IPO before the end of 2026, with a proposed ticker of ANT.
If that timeline holds, OpenAI’s chief rival would hit public markets roughly a year ahead of it.
Both companies are also chasing the same customers. Anthropic made inroads with businesses early, and OpenAI’s recent enterprise surge looks, at least in part, like a response to that.

For investors, the clearest signal is that OpenAI wants to be judged as a business software company, not a consumer app. Enterprise revenue becoming its primary source is the story it appears to be building for public market buyers.
That story has supporting data. A 70% jump in run rate and more than doubled enterprise sales in a single quarter are the kind of figures that make underwriters smile politely in meetings.

There are also reasons for caution. Brockman said “I think so,” not “we will.” No date, exchange, or price has been set, and the company already pushed its timeline once after concluding 2026 was too early.
The shrinking private fundraising target is another detail worth tracking.

Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads. In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.” “We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said. He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share. “We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.” By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point. Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue. “And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with. Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul. “A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.
“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”

By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.

extraction.body: In the wake of the Republicans' historic defeat in the U.S. midterm elections and the Democratic "blue wave" that swept the country, The New York Times reported Thursday that a breakthrough may be possible in negotiations to end the war between the United States and Iran. Citing five officials familiar with the talks, including American and Iranian officials, the newspaper reported that Tehran was considering a series of proposals presented by mediators that could shape the future of its nuclear program. According to the report, which highlighted Qatar's mediation efforts between Tehran and Washington, Iran's willingness to reengage in nuclear negotiations after weeks of refusing to soften its position suggests that recent Qatari-led diplomatic efforts to prevent a return to all-out war have achieved some success. The officials told the newspaper that the terms now being considered to end the conflict amounted to "concrete proposals." Meanwhile, Russian media reported that President Vladimir Putin met in Moscow with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. "We held consultations with Putin on important regional issues," Rezaei said following the meeting, according to the reports. "The supreme leader asked me to convey his message to Putin as soon as possible. He replaced Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who had assumed the role in March following the killing of Ali Larijani, a longtime central figure in Iran's leadership, in an Israeli strike during Operation Roaring Lion. "We held important discussions concerning the postwar period and regional security arrangements," Rezaei said. "President Putin condemned the attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and regarded the war against Iran as unjust. He declared that he would do everything in his power to help bring the war to an end." Rezaei added that the meeting also addressed the possibility of constructing gas pipelines from Russia to Iran, a project intended to alleviate Iran's domestic gas shortages while allowing Russian gas to be sold to neighboring countries. An Iranian source described as knowledgeable about the talks told Lebanon's Hezbollah-affiliated Al Mayadeen television network that Rezaei had made clear Tehran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions were met and would not negotiate over that decision. Chief among them was the war with Iran, followed by the rising cost of living, the failure to implement what voters expected from an "America First" policy and the relationship between the United States and Israel. Trump later acknowledged that his vice president was largely correct but insisted that the war had been worth the cost. "I think that's largely true, because the war did cause some increase in gasoline prices in the short term," Trump said of Vance's assessment. "But at the same time, if I had to make the decision again, I would have to do exactly the same thing, because in the long term, that's the only solution. Iran must not be allowed to have a nuclear weapon." Nevertheless, White House officials and staff told Reuters overnight that Vance's post had surprised many in Washington. According to the report, White House officials had been informed of the post before its publication, but one official described it as a departure from Trump's position, even though the president acknowledged that his deputy was largely right. American officials who spoke to Reuters said the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran was still under consideration despite the Republicans' midterm defeat, and perhaps even because of it. According to two sources familiar with the matter, Trump received a briefing last week from Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, on possible options for resuming military operations against Iran, with no clear diplomatic path to ending the conflict in sight. U.S. intelligence assessments in recent months, according to an intelligence official and two other senior American officials, indicate that renewed strikes would not substantially change Tehran's negotiating position and would be even less likely to bring about the collapse of the Iranian regime. Despite those assessments, officials familiar with the deliberations warned that Trump could still order military action. They noted that he had been aware of the political risks ahead of the midterm elections but "simply didn't care." One source told Reuters that the likelihood of renewed fighting could now be greater because Trump has "nothing to lose politically" with the elections behind him. The source assessed that the president could adopt a tougher position toward Iran and move to resume strikes. Another source agreed that renewed military operations were now the most likely scenario, saying: "He's planning to bomb Iran. We asked him to wait until after the elections." In any event, Israel is preparing for every possibility, and the IDF has already begun preparations for a potential return to war with the Islamic Republic. One senior Israeli official said Trump "could ignore them and attack simply to show that he's strong and doesn't care about the election results." Another Israeli source familiar with the situation stressed: "There is no way to predict Trump's behavior."

extraction.body: President Donald Trump and his national security team on Monday discussed Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. lifts its blockade and the war ends, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed. The proposal would postpone negotiations on Tehran's nuclear ambitions for a later date, Axios and The Associated Press reported earlier Monday. It remains unclear if Trump, who has vowed not to lift the blockade until a deal with Iran is " 100% complete ," will entertain the reported offer to end the two-month-old war. "I will confirm the president has met with his national security team this morning," Leavitt said at a press briefing Monday afternoon when asked about the reports. "The meeting may be ongoing," Leavitt said around 1:23 p.m. ET, "but the proposal was being discussed." "I don't want to get ahead of the president or his national security team. What I will reiterate is that the president's red lines with respect to Iran have been made very, very clear, not just to the American public, but also to them as well." Leavitt quickly added she was not saying that Trump and his team are "considering" the offer. "I would just say that there was a discussion this morning that I don't want to get ahead of, and you'll hear directly from the president, I'm sure on this topic, very soon," she said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a Fox News interview earlier Monday appeared to pour cold water on any Iranian proposal to clear the strategically vital strait. "What they mean by opening the straits is, 'Yes, the straits are open, as long as you coordinate with Iran, get our permission, or we'll blow you up and you pay us,'" Rubio said, when asked about Trump's claim Saturday that Iran had sent a "much better" offer. "That's not opening the straits. Those are international waterways. They cannot normalize, nor can we tolerate them trying to normalize, a system in which the Iranians decide who gets to use an international waterway and how much you have to pay them to use it," Rubio said. The Trump administration has repeatedly insisted the central goal of the conflict is keeping Iran from ever obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Everything will be peanuts compared to that, if they ever were given a nuclear weapon," Trump said Saturday night when he spoke to reporters at the White House after a shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner. But efforts at a diplomatic solution appeared to hit a sudden roadblock over the weekend. Trump on Saturday canceled plans for his son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff to meet with their Iranian counterparts in Pakistan. "Too much time wasted on traveling, too much work!" he wrote in a Truth Social post , while asserting the U.S. still has "all the cards." Trump announced the decision after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had departed Islamabad after only speaking with Pakistani officials, Reuters reported . And interestingly, immediately, when I canceled it, within 10 minutes, we got a new paper that was much better," Trump said before boarding Air Force One on Saturday, Bloomberg reported . Vance was not included in the latest travel plans. A U.S.-Iran ceasefire remains in effect after Trump unilaterally extended it last week. But the two sides throughout the truce have continued to jockey for advantage over each other, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as the main battleground. The strait, a vital shipping route that in normal times ferries 20% of the world's oil, remains Iran's main source of leverage in the ongoing conflict. Tehran effectively closed the passage through force, with just a small fraction of prewar ship traffic making it through. The de facto closure has sent oil prices spiraling , leading to higher prices for gasoline and other products in the U.S. and around the world. passages: US President Donald Trump met with his top national security advisers Thursday to discuss Iran for the first time since the midterm elections, Axios reported, citing two US officials.
Trump said a decision on whether to resume major military strikes would come soon.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X that Iran had inflicted a strategic defeat on Trump on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as a political defeat in Washington.

According to Axios, Trump is considering three options: launching new strikes, maintaining economic pressure on Tehran or pursuing a diplomatic agreement that would require significant US concessions.

An Iran International investigation in October showed Iran had executed nearly two people a week in political and security cases since the January protests, including over protest- and war-related accusations, while another 190 people faced death sentences.
According to Rezaei, Putin condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran, including strikes on its nuclear facilities, and offered Russian assistance in ending the war.
A US official told Axios that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was finalizing preparations for possible major combat operations against Iran but had received no new directive from Washington.

The question facing Iranian policymakers is whether Trump's electoral setback offers a chance to secure concessions or whether maintaining pressure will yield better terms, and how long Iran can afford to wait.
Nima Akbarkhani, another regular panellist, criticised reformists who had expected Biden to restore the 2015 nuclear agreement after Trump withdrew from it in 2018.
Although Biden returned the United States to several international agreements abandoned by Trump, his administration did not rejoin the nuclear deal.
Arrested on January 14, he was sentenced to death in August on national security-related charges.
“Now we will make a decision,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to.
The commentators also warned against repeating what they regarded as misplaced optimism following Joe Biden's victory over Trump in 2020.

The competing assessments come as Tehran pursues diplomatic contacts beyond Washington. The question facing Iranian policymakers is whether Trump's electoral setback offers a chance to secure concessions or whether maintaining pressure will yield better terms, and how long Iran can afford to wait. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei dismissed hopes that changes in the balance of power in Washington could lead to a softer American approach. In a message published Wednesday to mark Iran's National Day of Fighting Global Arrogance, Khamenei described as "seriously mistaken" those who retain "even the slightest hope for a change in behavior or shifts in political parties and factions" in the United States. He warned that even a limited inclination toward surrender would weaken the government's domestic support and encourage further American demands. Senior Iranian officials and pro-establishment media have portrayed the Democrats' gains as a consequence of the political and economic costs of the war. Khazab pointed to rising gasoline, diesel and fertiliser prices, arguing that the war had contributed to Republican losses in agricultural states such as Iowa and Kansas. The commentators also warned against repeating what they regarded as misplaced optimism following Joe Biden's victory over Trump in 2020. Nima Akbarkhani, another regular panellist, criticised reformists who had expected Biden to restore the 2015 nuclear agreement after Trump withdrew from it in 2018. Although Biden returned the United States to several international agreements abandoned by Trump, his administration did not rejoin the nuclear deal. "Why didn't he return to the JCPOA?" Akbarkhani asked, referring to the agreement by its formal abbreviation. "Because they were telling themselves that this was once again the time to enter new negotiations and secure further concessions." Iran stepped up diplomatic efforts on Thursday, submitting a new nuclear proposal to Washington, seeking Russian support and reaching out to regional powers a day after President Donald Trump's party suffered a sweeping defeat in the US midterm elections. Tehran sent Washington a nuclear proposal through Qatar, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official who said any discussion of its contents would depend on the United States first meeting Iran's seven demands. The official said Washington was reviewing the proposal. Rezaei told Iranian state television that Khamenei had wanted the message conveyed to Putin as soon as possible. He did not disclose its contents. According to Rezaei, Putin condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran, including strikes on its nuclear facilities, and offered Russian assistance in ending the war. "He believed this was an unjust war and that it should end as soon as possible," Rezaei said. "He said, 'We are ready to cooperate in any way we can to help end the war.'" Matin Shabani and Amir Delshad were sentenced by Branch 5 of the Mashhad Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Hossein Yazdankhah, according to the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA). An Iran International review of cases involving political charges found that approximately 220 prisoners are currently under sentence of death across Iran, up from around 194 previously reported. Shabani was convicted of moharebeh , or "waging war against God", over allegations of arson and destruction of public property during protests in Shandiz, near Mashhad. In another case, Pouria Hosseini-Mofrad, 23, has appealed his death sentence to Iran's Supreme Court, HRANA reported. Arrested on January 14, he was sentenced to death in August on national security-related charges. A source cited by HRANA said the allegations against him included breaking the glass of a bus stop and setting fire to shrubs. HRANA also identified 34-year-old Vahid Khedrikhah as one of three protesters sentenced to death in a separate joint case. Human Rights Watch and the Abdorrahman Boroumand Center said in September that authorities were using rushed proceedings, torture-tainted confessions and public executions to instill fear and deter dissent. Their review found that 16 of 29 protest-related execution cases involved no allegation of killing. An Iran International investigation in October showed Iran had executed nearly two people a week in political and security cases since the January protests, including over protest- and war-related accusations, while another 190 people faced death sentences. At least 70 people were executed from January 7 to October 5. Human rights organizations and activists say the figures are minimum totals, covering only cases that have been reported and verified.
