coreStoryFacts.text: President Donald Trump and his national security team on Monday discussed Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. lifts its blockade and the war ends, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed.

"Everything will be peanuts compared to that, if they ever were given a nuclear weapon," Trump said Saturday night when he spoke to reporters at the White House after a shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner.

"What they mean by opening the straits is, 'Yes, the straits are open, as long as you coordinate with Iran, get our permission, or we'll blow you up and you pay us,'" Rubio said, when asked about Trump's claim Saturday that Iran had sent a "much better" offer.
It remains unclear if Trump, who has vowed not to lift the blockade until a deal with Iran is " 100% complete ," will entertain the reported offer to end the two-month-old war.
A U.S.-Iran ceasefire remains in effect after Trump unilaterally extended it last week.
Tehran effectively closed the passage through force, with just a small fraction of prewar ship traffic making it through.
"They gave us a paper that should have been better.
And interestingly, immediately, when I canceled it, within 10 minutes, we got a new paper that was much better," Trump said before boarding Air Force One on Saturday, Bloomberg reported .
What I will reiterate is that the president's red lines with respect to Iran have been made very, very clear, not just to the American public, but also to them as well."
The cancellation ended immediate prospects for a second round of peace talks with Iran.
Trump has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports in the region.
At least 38 ships have been stopped or turned around so far, U.S.
Trump on Saturday canceled plans for his son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff to meet with their Iranian counterparts in Pakistan.
Trump announced the decision after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had departed Islamabad after only speaking with Pakistani officials, Reuters reported .
Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a Fox News interview earlier Monday appeared to pour cold water on any Iranian proposal to clear the strategically vital strait.

extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (WFLA) -- An Orlando man was identified as the person who drove a car into a courtyard at Citibank plaza in Tampa on Wednesday and fatally shot a woman. Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said that Jacob Pearson, 35, was being sued by Citibank over a $2,500 delinquent payment and contacted their attorneys that morning with a threatening message. "Unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15, my bulletproof vest and my insanity, you M-F'ing cancel this court case," Pearson said, according to Chronister. They're only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is F with me." The attorney's office reported the threat to Citibank's head of security, who contacted the Orlando Police Department. OPD then contacted the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, who sent a supervisor and deputy to the Citibank campus, which is located near East Dr. When they arrived, the supervisor called Citibank security to coordinate, and during the call, the security officer reported hearing gunshots. "The security officer says, 'courtyard, courtyard!' and hangs up the phone," Chronister said. Pearson crashed his car into a fence and drove into the courtyard, which was next to the cafeteria. He got out of the car with a rifle, approached the first person he saw, and shot her three times before the rifle malfunctioned. "This suspect walks back to his car, retrieves his handgun, walks back over to the victim, who's trying to crawl away with her life, and executes her," Chronister said. Security camera video showed Pearson walking into the cafeteria, where just moments before, many of the complex's 3,000 employees were having lunch. Chronister said they heard the gunshots and fled, with some leaving purses, glasses and even their shoes behind. Pearson proceeded into the main building, where a security officer, identified as John Fraley, was waiting for him. "This is our hero, this Citibank employee, who runs towards danger," Chronister said. Fraley, a Marine Corp veteran, shot at Pearson, and Pearson returned fire. Farley shot at him again, striking him five times. "This suspect was armed with 90 rounds of ammunition. As you see in that cafeteria, he was intent on one purpose, and that purpose was to hunt any human being he could find and kill them," Chronister said. "Because of the heroic actions of this security officer ... his reign of terror ended before it even began." Pearson later succumbed to his injuries at Tampa General Hospital. The victim, identified as Leanne Selman, 41, died at the scene. More than 300 HCSO deputies responded to the active shooter call and worked to search the large corporate campus and evacuate employees. "I'm always concerned about my kids or schools," Dormarice Perez said. Never thought it was going to happen at the campus." "Something in my heart was like, this isn't normal," Stephanie Urra said.

The gunman then got out of his vehicle with a rifle and fatally shot a woman. An armed security guard employed by Citibank shot the suspect inside a nearby building's cafeteria during a gunfire exchange, authorities said. The gunman was taken to Tampa General Hospital where he later died. "The security guard that's employed by Citibank stopped the threat," Losat said. So kudos to that security guard and the people they employ." Four people were also treated at a local hospital for injuries that were not life-threatening. It is unclear where the victims were wounded during the incident. At the time the chaotic scene broke out, there were 3,200 Citibank employees on the property, Losat said. "With that being said, with that many witnesses… we will be doing interviews well into the night," Losat said. Our crime scene will be processing the scene, which will take several hours, if not until tomorrow." Losat did not release the name of the suspected gunman or the victim, pending notification to the next of kin. Authorities have cleared the Citibank property. Citibank employees were asked to meet at the triage area in the parking lot of the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel. "The low-rise campus is surrounded by lushly landscaped berms with outdoor plazas, fountains, and waterfalls to provide a secluded, tranquil environment," the website states. "Each building is interconnected by enclosed walkways to ensure personnel comfort and building security as well as provide a homogenous atmosphere among the individual buildings and associated staff." "Phenomenal job by everyone collaboratively coming together to make sure that this tragic incident wasn't catastrophic," Chronister said during a press briefing on Thursday. "Our suspect took one life, and that's one life too many." Do you understand me? They are only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is f with me." Pearson had already left by the time officers arrived at this Orlando residence, according to the sheriff. His wife told police she did not know where he went but that he "appeared to be angry," Chronister said. Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said that Jacob Pearson, 35, was being sued by Citibank over a $2,500 delinquent payment and contacted their attorneys that morning with a threatening message. "Unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15, my bulletproof vest and my insanity, you M-F'ing cancel this court case," Pearson said, according to Chronister. They're only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is F with me." The attorney's office reported the threat to Citibank's head of security, who contacted the Orlando Police Department. OPD then contacted the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, who sent a supervisor and deputy to the Citibank campus, which is located near East Dr. When they arrived, the supervisor called Citibank security to coordinate, and during the call, the security officer reported hearing gunshots. "The security officer says, 'courtyard, courtyard!' and hangs up the phone," Chronister said. Pearson crashed his car into a fence and drove into the courtyard, which was next to the cafeteria. He got out of the car with a rifle, approached the first person he saw, and shot her three times before the rifle malfunctioned. "This suspect walks back to his car, retrieves his handgun, walks back over to the victim, who's trying to crawl away with her life, and executes her," Chronister said. Security camera video showed Pearson walking into the cafeteria, where just moments before, many of the complex's 3,000 employees were having lunch. Chronister said they heard the gunshots and fled, with some leaving purses, glasses and even their shoes behind. Pearson proceeded into the main building, where a security officer, identified as John Fraley, was waiting for him. "This is our hero, this Citibank employee, who runs towards danger," Chronister said. Fraley, a Marine Corp veteran, shot at Pearson, and Pearson returned fire. Farley shot at him again, striking him five times. "This suspect was armed with 90 rounds of ammunition. As you see in that cafeteria, he was intent on one purpose, and that purpose was to hunt any human being he could find and kill them," Chronister said. "Because of the heroic actions of this security officer ... his reign of terror ended before it even began." Pearson later succumbed to his injuries at Tampa General Hospital. The victim, identified as Leanne Selman, 41, died at the scene. More than 300 HCSO deputies responded to the active shooter call and worked to search the large corporate campus and evacuate employees. "I'm always concerned about my kids or schools," Dormarice Perez said. Never thought it was going to happen at the campus." "Something in my heart was like, this isn't normal," Stephanie Urra said.

Hours after allegedly threatening violence against the company, authorities say he crashed his vehicle into the courtyard of the Tampa-area Citibank office complex and opened fire, fatally shooting the first person he saw and sparking panic on the large campus. Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister said there likely would have been more casualties if not for the heroic actions of a Citibank security guard, who shot and killed the gunman after he entered a cafeteria armed with a rifle. "Phenomenal job by everyone collaboratively coming together to make sure that this tragic incident wasn't catastrophic," Chronister said during a press briefing on Thursday. "Our suspect took one life, and that's one life too many." Chronister identified the suspect in Wednesday's shooting as 35-year-old Jacob Pearson, a married father of one with no criminal record, who lived in Orlando. "This was targeted; he targeted Citibank employees yesterday, holding them responsible for his debt," Chronister said. Around 9 a.m. Wednesday, Pearson contacted an attorney's office contracted by Citibank for collection, "upset" and "irate" that he recently received a summons to go to court over a delinquent payment, according to Chronister. According to the sheriff, Pearson allegedly told the attorney's office, "Unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15, my bulletproof vest, and my insanity ... cancel this court case. Do you understand me? They are only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is f with me." Pearson had already left by the time officers arrived at this Orlando residence, according to the sheriff. His wife told police she did not know where he went but that he "appeared to be angry," Chronister said. Orlando police updated the head of security at Citibank, who contacted the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office to report the threat, saying, "We don't know where he's at. We don't know if he intends on following up on that threat," according to Chronister. The Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office dispatched two law enforcement officers to the Citibank campus, and while coordinating with the Citibank security team on where to go, gunshots were fired in the courtyard shortly after noon, according to Chronister. The suspect had crashed his vehicle through a gate in the courtyard, exited it carrying a rifle and walked toward the first Citibank employee that he saw and shot her three times, according to the sheriff. "As he shoots her, his rifle begins to malfunction," Chronister said. "This suspect returns back to his car, retrieves his handgun, walks back over to the victim, who's trying to crawl away with her life, and executes her." passages: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has appointed Brian Bonacci to lead its emergency communications division and named Brian Mazanec acting executive assistant director for infrastructure security .
As acting EAD of CISA’s infrastructure security division, Mazanec will help lead the agency’s nationwide work to safeguard critical infrastructure against all hazards.
He will focus on risk management and resilience, partnering with members of the critical infrastructure community.

His work included directing responses to cyberattacks affecting the healthcare and public health sectors, including the 2024 Change Healthcare incident, as well as the 2026 hantavirus and Bundibugyo Ebola responses.
He also worked with CISA and the FBI on joint cybersecurity advisories and engaged critical infrastructure partners.
Butera succeeds Nick Andersen, who took over as acting CISA director after DHS named Gottumukkala its director of strategic implementation.

extraction.body: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has appointed Brian Bonacci to lead its emergency communications division and named Brian Mazanec acting executive assistant director for infrastructure security . CISA announced the appointments separately on LinkedIn Wednesday. Strengthening critical infrastructure requires coordination among federal agencies, industry partners and the organizations responsible for essential services. The Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Homeland Security Summit , happening in just six days on Nov. 10, will examine how agencies can use advanced technologies to address cybersecurity and physical security threats. DHS Deputy Secretary Troy Edgar is scheduled to keynote the event. Save your seat at the summit . Bonacci will serve as executive assistant director for emergency communications, after previously holding the position in an acting capacity this year. He initially joined CISA in 2025 as chief of staff before serving as a senior counselor to the secretary at the Department of Homeland Security, providing insight on cybersecurity and infrastructure security. Then-acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala swore Bonacci in as chief of staff in August 2025, tasking him with overseeing strategy, planning and resource allocation in support of the agency’s mission. As acting EAD of CISA’s infrastructure security division, Mazanec will help lead the agency’s nationwide work to safeguard critical infrastructure against all hazards. He will focus on risk management and resilience, partnering with members of the critical infrastructure community. Bonacci’s career spans more than three decades in federal IT and telecommunications. Before joining CISA, he founded gScale Consulting and served as senior vice president of growth at RIVA Solutions. He was director of public sector partnerships at ScienceLogic, director of federal partnerships & channels at Equinix for three years and senior director of government markets at Infinera. Bonacci also spent nearly five years at Level 3 Communications, where he served multiple leadership positions spanning government advocacy, business operations and industry relations. He also held leadership roles at TW Telecom, Qwest, Unisys, SAIC and Verizon . He served as systems analyst at the Internal Revenue Service’s Systems Integration Office, where he developed strategies and architectures for the Tax Systems Modernization Program. He began his public service career as a computer scientist at the U.S. General Accounting Office. He has also been active in professional associations, including the Government Business Executive Forum, the Advanced Technology Academic Research Center and the Independent Telecommunications Pioneer Association. Mazanec brings over two decades of experience in risk assessment, all-hazards preparedness and critical infrastructure security. He was previously affiliated with the Department of Health and Human Services’ Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, where he served as deputy assistant secretary and director of the Center for Preparedness. At HHS, he led operational coordination and response activities for emergencies and disasters. His work included directing responses to cyberattacks affecting the healthcare and public health sectors, including the 2024 Change Healthcare incident, as well as the 2026 hantavirus and Bundibugyo Ebola responses. He also worked with CISA and the FBI on joint cybersecurity advisories and engaged critical infrastructure partners. Mazanec was also part of GAO early in his career, overseeing the agency’s strategic warfare, security and intelligence portfolio. He also specialized in weapons of mass destruction matters at the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Nuclear Matters and the Joint Staff. Bonacci and Mazanec’s appointments follow CISA’s selection of Chris Butera as acting EAD of its cybersecurity division . Butera succeeds Nick Andersen, who took over as acting CISA director after DHS named Gottumukkala its director of strategic implementation. sources.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
passages: However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.

And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring.

Details The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday, November 5, 2026, down 5.5%, its worst session since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 (the index of the hundred largest non-financial stocks on the exchange) lost 6.4% and $2.5 trillion in market value. The selling, two days after the American midterm elections, was triggered by fears that the Democratic victory will slow the construction of data centers for artificial intelligence. The bill was paid by the companies at the heart of that buildout. Micron (server memory) and AMD (AI processors and accelerators, a rival to Nvidia) each gave up 17%, while CoreWeave, a "neocloud" (a company that rents out computing power for AI and has grown largely on borrowed money), shed 10%. The vote, the local referendums and the change of hands in Congress are covered in our piece on the midterms and artificial intelligence . In defense tech, meanwhile, Shield AI is buying counter-drone radar maker Echodyne for $5.3 billion . On November 5, 2026 the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, the S&P 500 4.4% and the Dow Jones more than 1,800 points (3.4%), according to data reported by CNBC . All eleven sectors of the S&P 500 closed in the red, but the heaviest blow landed on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Midway through the session Fortune was already counting more than $3 trillion wiped off the Composite and a chip index heading for its worst day since March 2020, the start of the pandemic. By the closing bell the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (SOX, the basket of the thirty largest listed chipmakers) was down 12% and at its lowest in more than six months, while the VIX, the gauge of expected volatility, posted its biggest jump since December 2024, as Reuters notes. Nvidia dropped 9% and, CNBC writes, is back in negative territory for the year. The "Magnificent Seven" of Big Tech lost more than $1 trillion between them. Tesla and SpaceX, Elon Musk's companies, shed $456 billion since Tuesday's close, though for CNBC their case has an extra twist, the fear of new congressional investigations and tougher regulation. Nvidia closed the November 5 session at $181.60, down 9.26%, on volume of 300 million shares (157% above its three-month average), according to The Motley Fool . The stock fell to its lowest level since April and is now down 2.5% for the year. Multiplied by the shares outstanding, the $18.53 drop per share comes to nearly $450 billion of market value erased in a single day, and the next test is the quarterly report on November 17. Data centers are the customers of the chipmakers. Every multibillion-dollar campus buys processors, memory and networking gear and consumes energy in vast quantities. If politics slows down permits, future demand for those components slips, and the market prices that in at once on Nvidia, AMD and Micron shares. Micron, which in early October forecast scarcer memory in 2027 and 2028 than in 2026 , is among the hardest hit. The estimates in circulation show how much is at stake. UBS analysts calculate that about 30% of the new data center capacity planned in the United States for 2028 is at risk from possible construction freezes (Reuters). Dan Ives, an analyst who is usually bullish on the sector, wrote that at least 10% of the 800 to 1,000 AI data centers in the pipeline will fall off schedule and that up to 20% will face a much longer approval process. In Ives's view the growth in Big Tech investment will peak in 2027 rather than in 2028 or 2029, even though spending will stay above $1 trillion. Neoclouds face a second pressure, debt. CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps (contracts the market uses to insure against a borrower's failure) hit a record 1,267.9 basis points. The stock closed down 10%. Nebius, another neocloud, lost 15%. Both have seen their value halve or worse since October 6, the day of the Nasdaq peak. Applied Digital, Cipher Digital and IREN, which run data centers, each fell by more than 14%. On top of that comes a Bloomberg report, picked up by Reuters, that Microsoft is stepping up oversight of some data center projects run by Nebius, IREN and Nscale. Microsoft shares closed down 3.6%. Even the suppliers of power and equipment were not spared. GE Vernova lost 7.4% and Constellation Energy 2.5%, while Amazon and Alphabet, which had held up on Wednesday, gave up 2.2% each. On Wednesday, at a Wall Street Journal conference, Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that building data centers in the United States "will be harder" and that every big cloud operator is asking whether it should build outside the country instead. The industry, she acknowledged, "has not explained the benefits of these investments well enough," as TechCrunch reports. Meta has data centers in 23 states, five of them planned as projects of at least one gigawatt. It expects projects to be judged more and more on local consent. Its template for deals that work has the company paying for its own electricity, directing the tax surplus to teachers and first responders, hiring local labor and seeking bipartisan backing. OpenAI, for its part, published a "National Community Compact" on Thursday, a pact with the communities that host its campuses. According to MAD Robot , which cites the company's documents, every campus OpenAI owns and operates will pay in full for its own electricity and the grid infrastructure it needs, will publish water and energy use site by site and will no longer ask public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs). An attached policy blueprint asks lawmakers to turn the same rules into law for the whole industry. Back on November 2 the company had announced, as Axios reports, that it intends to cut up to one gigawatt of consumption (roughly 700,000 homes) when the grid is under strain, starting with the Effingham County campus in Georgia. NDAs were already in the crosshairs. Amazon Web Services had dropped them with public agencies on October 2, announcing a community program worth more than $1 billion, as we reported in Amazon drops NDAs on data centers . OpenAI's text, MAD Robot notes, does not mention the elections, but it lands two days after the vote. On Friday, November 6, Asian markets, where much of the AI hardware is made, followed Wall Street lower. According to CNBC's live coverage , Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 5.9% and entered a "bear market" (at least 20% below its June high), while South Korea's Kospi fell by more than 6% after triggering automatic trading halts in the early hours. The selling hit the entire supply chain. In detail, SK Hynix lost more than 8%, Samsung Electronics 7%, TSMC 9.6%, Foxconn 9.4%, Advantest (a maker of chip testing machines) 12.2%, SoftBank Group 11.6% and Kioxia almost 10%. The Hong Kong market held up better, with the Hang Seng down 1%. Both. The difference matters. The Nasdaq 100 had already closed Monday, November 2, more than 10% below its October 6 record, in correction before the polls even opened, because investors feared that spending on AI infrastructure was running ahead of revenue, Reuters points out. Intel's 30% plunge, which we covered in Intel plunges 30%, tech stocks burn through $1 trillion , had set off the selling as early as October 30, and the International Monetary Fund had warned about AI-related debt in AI bubble, the IMF warns about $650 billion in debt . In China the STAR50, Shanghai's tech index, had already lost 40%, as we wrote when discussing the Chinese AI bubble . President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that the market "suffered one of the worst days in history" because of the outcome of the vote. The traders Reuters spoke to are split on how to read it. For Michael O'Rourke of JonesTrading the data center slowdown is "the theme that will stay," while Ted Parkhill of Incline Investment Management describes a market moving "from the promise of AI to the price of AI." Simeon Wallis of Aprio Wealth Management, speaking to Fortune, warns instead that markets can overreact in the short term. The most concrete front is Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX are preparing the Terafab complex (chips and data centers) and where Wells Fargo places 27% of the data center gigawatts planned in the United States. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told CNN that we need to "stop what we are doing with data centers" until there are protections in place for Texans. She also asked to suspend negotiations over the sale of public land to SpaceX. A moratorium is not automatic, because the Texas legislature remains Republican, as our midterms piece explains. Meta, for its part, says it receives requests every day to rent the computing power it has already built, and so sees, one way or another, a path to earning back the investment. In forty-eight hours the market found out that a data center is also a political object. For the past two years it had been only engineering and finance. Now it has a constituency. The Nasdaq Composite is in a correction, not a bear market. A correction is a drop of at least 10% from a recent high; the Composite, according to Reuters, has lost almost 12% from the record it closed at on October 6. A bear market usually starts beyond 20%, a threshold CNBC says the Nikkei 225 has crossed relative to its June peak. Because they fund themselves with debt, at a time when money costs more. Reuters recalls that American interest rates have risen since the end of summer and that the ability of companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius to raise funds was already limited. Alphabet, backed by Google's advertising business, closed down 2.2%, against CoreWeave's 10%. No, not yet. No new federal law will arrive before 2027, and the bans voted by residents concern individual municipalities, as we explain in the midterms piece . The market has mostly priced in the direction of travel, meaning more oversight, more time to get permits and rising costs. For now there is only doubt, no announced delay. Reuters writes that some analysts wonder whether the scale of the selloff could affect the timing of Anthropic's listing, expected in the fall. The ticker ANT is already confirmed, as we wrote in Anthropic shares, the ticker ANT is confirmed . The figures from the prospectus are in Anthropic IPO, the prospectus reveals AI close to accelerating its own research . Nobody knows in advance, and this is not investment advice. The first hard data point arrives on November 17 with quarterly results, when Nvidia will say how many data center chips it sold and what it expects for the coming months. Until then the stock stays tied to the same question that sank the Nasdaq, namely whether permits for new data centers will slow after the vote. The Nasdaq 100 had already closed Monday, November 2, more than 10% below its October 6 record, in correction before the polls even opened, because investors feared that spending on AI infrastructure was running ahead of revenue, Reuters points out. Intel's 30% plunge, which we covered in Intel plunges 30%, tech stocks burn through $1 trillion , had set off the selling as early as October 30, and the International Monetary Fund had warned about AI-related debt in AI bubble, the IMF warns about $650 billion in debt . President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that the market "suffered one of the worst days in history" because of the outcome of the vote. The traders Reuters spoke to are split on how to read it. For Michael O'Rourke of JonesTrading the data center slowdown is "the theme that will stay," while Ted Parkhill of Incline Investment Management describes a market moving "from the promise of AI to the price of AI." Simeon Wallis of Aprio Wealth Management, speaking to Fortune, warns instead that markets can overreact in the short term.

The most concrete front is Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX are preparing the Terafab complex (chips and data centers) and where Wells Fargo places 27% of the data center gigawatts planned in the United States. Meta, for its part, says it receives requests every day to rent the computing power it has already built, and so sees, one way or another, a path to earning back the investment.
In forty-eight hours the market found out that a data center is also a political object. For the past two years it had been only engineering and finance. Now it has a constituency.

The Nasdaq Composite is in a correction, not a bear market. A correction is a drop of at least 10% from a recent high; the Composite, according to Reuters, has lost almost 12% from the record it closed at on October 6. A bear market usually starts beyond 20%, a threshold CNBC says the Nikkei 225 has crossed relative to its June peak.

Because they fund themselves with debt, at a time when money costs more. No, not yet. No new federal law will arrive before 2027, and the bans voted by residents concern individual municipalities, as we explain in the midterms piece . The market has mostly priced in the direction of travel, meaning more oversight, more time to get permits and rising costs.

The selling, two days after the American midterm elections, was triggered by fears that the Democratic victory will slow the construction of data centers for artificial intelligence. The bill was paid by the companies at the heart of that buildout. Micron (server memory) and AMD (AI processors and accelerators, a rival to Nvidia) each gave up 17%, while CoreWeave, a "neocloud" (a company that rents out computing power for AI and has grown largely on borrowed money), shed 10%. The vote, the local referendums and the change of hands in Congress are covered in our piece on the midterms and artificial intelligence . In defense tech, meanwhile, Shield AI is buying counter-drone radar maker Echodyne for $5.3 billion . On November 5, 2026 the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, the S&P 500 4.4% and the Dow Jones more than 1,800 points (3.4%), according to data reported by CNBC . All eleven sectors of the S&P 500 closed in the red, but the heaviest blow landed on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Midway through the session Fortune was already counting more than $3 trillion wiped off the Composite and a chip index heading for its worst day since March 2020, the start of the pandemic. By the closing bell the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (SOX, the basket of the thirty largest listed chipmakers) was down 12% and at its lowest in more than six months, while the VIX, the gauge of expected volatility, posted its biggest jump since December 2024, as Reuters notes. Nvidia dropped 9% and, CNBC writes, is back in negative territory for the year. The "Magnificent Seven" of Big Tech lost more than $1 trillion between them. Tesla and SpaceX, Elon Musk's companies, shed $456 billion since Tuesday's close, though for CNBC their case has an extra twist, the fear of new congressional investigations and tougher regulation. Nvidia closed the November 5 session at $181.60, down 9.26%, on volume of 300 million shares (157% above its three-month average), according to The Motley Fool . The stock fell to its lowest level since April and is now down 2.5% for the year. Multiplied by the shares outstanding, the $18.53 drop per share comes to nearly $450 billion of market value erased in a single day, and the next test is the quarterly report on November 17. Data centers are the customers of the chipmakers. Every multibillion-dollar campus buys processors, memory and networking gear and consumes energy in vast quantities. If politics slows down permits, future demand for those components slips, and the market prices that in at once on Nvidia, AMD and Micron shares. Micron, which in early October forecast scarcer memory in 2027 and 2028 than in 2026 , is among the hardest hit. The estimates in circulation show how much is at stake. UBS analysts calculate that about 30% of the new data center capacity planned in the United States for 2028 is at risk from possible construction freezes (Reuters). Dan Ives, an analyst who is usually bullish on the sector, wrote that at least 10% of the 800 to 1,000 AI data centers in the pipeline will fall off schedule and that up to 20% will face a much longer approval process. In Ives's view the growth in Big Tech investment will peak in 2027 rather than in 2028 or 2029, even though spending will stay above $1 trillion. Neoclouds face a second pressure, debt. CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps (contracts the market uses to insure against a borrower's failure) hit a record 1,267.9 basis points. The stock closed down 10%. Nebius, another neocloud, lost 15%. Both have seen their value halve or worse since October 6, the day of the Nasdaq peak. Applied Digital, Cipher Digital and IREN, which run data centers, each fell by more than 14%. On top of that comes a Bloomberg report, picked up by Reuters, that Microsoft is stepping up oversight of some data center projects run by Nebius, IREN and Nscale. Microsoft shares closed down 3.6%. Even the suppliers of power and equipment were not spared. GE Vernova lost 7.4% and Constellation Energy 2.5%, while Amazon and Alphabet, which had held up on Wednesday, gave up 2.2% each. On Wednesday, at a Wall Street Journal conference, Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that building data centers in the United States "will be harder" and that every big cloud operator is asking whether it should build outside the country instead. The industry, she acknowledged, "has not explained the benefits of these investments well enough," as TechCrunch reports. Meta has data centers in 23 states, five of them planned as projects of at least one gigawatt. It expects projects to be judged more and more on local consent. Its template for deals that work has the company paying for its own electricity, directing the tax surplus to teachers and first responders, hiring local labor and seeking bipartisan backing. OpenAI, for its part, published a "National Community Compact" on Thursday, a pact with the communities that host its campuses. According to MAD Robot , which cites the company's documents, every campus OpenAI owns and operates will pay in full for its own electricity and the grid infrastructure it needs, will publish water and energy use site by site and will no longer ask public officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs). An attached policy blueprint asks lawmakers to turn the same rules into law for the whole industry. Back on November 2 the company had announced, as Axios reports, that it intends to cut up to one gigawatt of consumption (roughly 700,000 homes) when the grid is under strain, starting with the Effingham County campus in Georgia. NDAs were already in the crosshairs. Amazon Web Services had dropped them with public agencies on October 2, announcing a community program worth more than $1 billion, as we reported in Amazon drops NDAs on data centers . OpenAI's text, MAD Robot notes, does not mention the elections, but it lands two days after the vote. On Friday, November 6, Asian markets, where much of the AI hardware is made, followed Wall Street lower. According to CNBC's live coverage , Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 5.9% and entered a "bear market" (at least 20% below its June high), while South Korea's Kospi fell by more than 6% after triggering automatic trading halts in the early hours. The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday, November 5, 2026, down 5.5%, its worst session since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 (the index of the hundred largest non-financial stocks on the exchange) lost 6.4% and $2.5 trillion in market value. The bill was paid by the companies at the heart of that buildout. Micron (server memory) and AMD (AI processors and accelerators, a rival to Nvidia) each gave up 17%, while CoreWeave, a "neocloud" (a company that rents out computing power for AI and has grown largely on borrowed money), shed 10%. The vote, the local referendums and the change of hands in Congress are covered in our piece on the midterms and artificial intelligence .
In defense tech, meanwhile, Shield AI is buying counter-drone radar maker Echodyne for $5.3 billion .

Midway through the session Fortune was already counting more than $3 trillion wiped off the Composite and a chip index heading for its worst day since March 2020, the start of the pandemic. Nvidia dropped 9% and, CNBC writes, is back in negative territory for the year. The "Magnificent Seven" of Big Tech lost more than $1 trillion between them. UBS analysts calculate that about 30% of the new data center capacity planned in the United States for 2028 is at risk from possible construction freezes (Reuters). passages: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily.
Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch.
Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal.
Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation.

Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents' access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch's competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.
Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli startup that tracks and secures the credentials AI agents use, for about $500 million.
Neither company has confirmed the deal or the price.
Several outlets add details that go beyond the confirmed core.
Another implies the price equals about 50 times Clutch Security’s annual recurring revenue.
A third cites a funding total near $28.5 million.
A fourth credits CEO Nikesh Arora with driving the deal as part of an AI security arms race.
That matters for the Clutch Security acquisition thesis.
Security spending follows deployment with a lag.
A buyer that moves while only a minority of companies run agents at scale is betting on 2027 and 2028 budgets, not 2026 ones.
The survey data supports that timing without proving it, and it dates from 2025, so the true share today may be higher.
A credential-control product for agents slots neatly into that pitch, because identity sits between nearly every other security layer.
Owning an agent-credential product lets the company claim a position in a topic that security buyers increasingly raise in budget meetings.
The reports do not say how large the additional payouts could be, how long they would run, or what Clutch Security would have to deliver to earn them.
The underlying risk exists today, whoever ends up owning Clutch Security.
Software agents now log in to corporate systems with passwords, tokens, API keys and service accounts, and most security teams cannot say how many of those secrets exist.
Demand for agent security depends on how many companies actually deploy agents.
Agent credential security draws players from four directions.
Agents blur all three, since an agent is software that moves across networks, workloads and identities in one session.

extraction.body: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight." Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. sources.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
passages: But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist.
I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.
At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit.

They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps.
As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far.
But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so.

Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists.
As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants.
But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help.

I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said. Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. sources.title: I hired a humanoid robot to help clean my home. An auntie did most of the chores - The Straits Times
passages: Many firms are training humanoids to do chores like fold clothes and tidy tables in data factories simulating home environments.
But X Square Robot, the Shenzhen-based creator of Quanta, is going further with its home cleaning service, a tie-up with life services platform 58.com.
Joyce ZK Lim is The Straits Times’ China correspondent, based in Shenzhen.
In time to come, it plans to expand what chores the robot can do, and make the service available in more cities.
They are part of a new cleaning service launched in China in March, as robot start-ups look beyond gongfu and dancing to make humanoids more useful in the real world.

As China grapples with an ageing workforce and declining birth rates, companies are betting on robots to be housekeepers for the future and bringing them into people’s homes to help them learn the job better.
China is the world’s largest producer and user of humanoid robots, a market which investment bank Barclays estimates could reach US$200 billion worldwide by 2035.
SHENZHEN – I opened my home last week to an unlikely trio: a boxy white robot named Quanta X1 Pro and its two human partners – housekeeper Aunty Tan and a young engineer .
A three-hour house-cleaning costs the same with or without the robot.
The robot’s last chore was to remove the used garbage bag from the trash can.
Then she wiped all the surfaces the robot did not clean.
Homes are notoriously tricky for humanoids to clean as the unpredictable environments are filled with finicky tasks.
Robots that can reliably do most household chores without supervision are, by most measures, at least a decade away, he added.
First the robot straightened two chairs at the dining table, grabbing their legs with its pincer-like hands and pushing them into place.

As China grapples with an ageing workforce and declining birth rates, companies are betting on robots to be housekeepers for the future and bringing them into people’s homes to help them learn the job better. Curious, I signed up for a three-hour cleaning service that costs 149 yuan (S$28), available in Shenzhen and Beijing. The cleaning is mainly still done by human hands, the engineer said as Aunty Tan bustled about the kitchen. For now, the 1.6m-tall robot fitted on a wheeled base with two mechanical arms would only perform simple tasks and operate in my living area. I watched as Quanta began by silently scanning the room to figure out what it could and would do. It works mostly autonomously, I was told, but would need help if it got stumped or stuck. The engineer, who declined to give his name, observed its every move, ready to step in if it hit a snag or broke anything. First the robot straightened two chairs at the dining table, grabbing their legs with its pincer-like hands and pushing them into place. The robot tidied my table tops and removed what it decided was trash – yes to a sweet wrapper and a folded leaflet; no to an empty box of Panadol. But instead of throwing both items together, it made two trips to the bin. I wanted to see if Quanta could wipe the dining table – something not part of its usual repertoire – so I set down a damp cloth and a spray bottle of detergent. The robot made wiping motions with the cloth but ignored the bottle, putting it aside as though in the way. It also left breadcrumbs on the table. Quanta wipes a table but could do a better job. The robot’s last chore was to remove the used garbage bag from the trash can. It did not succeed: the bag was probably too full and got stuck, surmised the engineer, who finished the job himself. He also had to help Quanta into my flat when it got stuck at the raised threshold, twice fixed a wire that came loose on its arm, and adjusted its spotty internet connection. The few things the robot did on its own, it did really slowly. In the time that it moseyed about my living room, Aunty Tan cleaned the rest of the flat. She washed the dirty dishes that the robot could not touch as its hands are not waterproof. She also cleaned the kitchen, scrubbed the toilet, mopped the floor and folded the remaining laundry. Then she wiped all the surfaces the robot did not clean. Asked what she thought of her humanoid partner, Aunty Tan was unimpressed. “Humans are still better at cleaning,” she said. “Look at the robot, what did it really do?” Homes are notoriously tricky for humanoids to clean as the unpredictable environments are filled with finicky tasks. The industry also lacks data to train them to be smarter faster. Many firms are training humanoids to do chores like fold clothes and tidy tables in data factories simulating home environments. But X Square Robot, the Shenzhen-based creator of Quanta, is going further with its home cleaning service, a tie-up with life services platform 58.com. To encourage people to open up their homes, the company offers Quanta’s services basically for free. A three-hour house-cleaning costs the same with or without the robot. Earlier on, the robot-inclusive version had even sold for half price to attract sign-ups. A fleet of robots has now worked in nearly 200 homes so far, the firm said. In time to come, it plans to expand what chores the robot can do, and make the service available in more cities. China is the world’s largest producer and user of humanoid robots, a market which investment bank Barclays estimates could reach US$200 billion worldwide by 2035. The country is gunning to deploy them in real-life settings ranging from factory floors to convenience stores, and now living rooms. In the city of Wuhan, Chinese firm GigaAI announced in May upcoming trials of its household humanoid in homes. Residents can apply to have a robot work for free in their homes next year, with priority given to families with old people, children or pets. Over in the United States, robots are also inching into homes. People can pay US$20,000 (S$25,600) to pre-order a household humanoid from start-up 1X Technologies, which is expected to ship this year. The company is upfront about collecting data from people’s homes. Firms are racing to rack up real-world training data as that is a big bottleneck for embodied AI at the moment, said Georg Stieler, head of robotics and automation at Stieler Technology & Market Advisory, a consultancy. Even as the sector rides a funding boom, companies recognise that their technology must improve quickly, “otherwise investors might become sceptical ”, he said. Robots that can reliably do most household chores without supervision are, by most measures, at least a decade away, he added. But in the interim, firms will jostle to put out robots that can do more and do better – with humans like Aunty Tan filling in the gap. The housekeeper did not rule out that the slow-moving humanoid might one day give her a run for her money. In 10 years, she reckoned, “this could all be different”. Joyce ZK Lim is The Straits Times’ China correspondent, based in Shenzhen.

Many firms are training humanoids to do chores like fold clothes and tidy tables in data factories simulating home environments. But X Square Robot, the Shenzhen-based creator of Quanta, is going further with its home cleaning service, a tie-up with life services platform 58.com.

To encourage people to open up their homes, the company offers Quanta’s services basically for free. A three-hour house-cleaning costs the same with or without the robot. Earlier on, the robot-inclusive version had even sold for half price to attract sign-ups.
A fleet of robots has now worked in nearly 200 homes so far, the firm said. In time to come, it plans to expand what chores the robot can do, and make the service available in more cities.

China is the world’s largest producer and user of humanoid robots, a market which investment bank Barclays estimates could reach US$200 billion worldwide by 2035. The country is gunning to deploy them in real-life settings ranging from factory floors to convenience stores, and now living rooms.

In the city of Wuhan, Chinese firm GigaAI announced in May upcoming trials of its household humanoid in homes. Residents can apply to have a robot work for free in their homes next year, with priority given to families with old people, children or pets.

Over in the United States, robots are also inching into homes. People can pay US$20,000 (S$25,600) to pre-order a household humanoid from start-up 1X Technologies, which is expected to ship this year. The company is upfront about collecting data from people’s homes.

Firms are racing to rack up real-world training data as that is a big bottleneck for embodied AI at the moment, said Georg Stieler, head of robotics and automation at Stieler Technology & Market Advisory, a consultancy.
Even as the sector rides a funding boom, companies recognise that their technology must improve quickly, “otherwise investors might become sceptical ”, he said.
Robots that can reliably do most household chores without supervision are, by most measures, at least a decade away, he added.
But in the interim, firms will jostle to put out robots that can do more and do better – with humans like Aunty Tan filling in the gap.
The housekeeper did not rule out that the slow-moving humanoid might one day give her a run for her money. In 10 years, she reckoned, “this could all be different”.
Joyce ZK Lim is The Straits Times’ China correspondent, based in Shenzhen.

They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps.
As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

extraction.body: The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning. I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out. Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI. I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.

As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

sources.title: I hired a humanoid robot to help clean my home. An auntie did most of the chores - The Straits Times
passages: Many firms are training humanoids to do chores like fold clothes and tidy tables in data factories simulating home environments.
But X Square Robot, the Shenzhen-based creator of Quanta, is going further with its home cleaning service, a tie-up with life services platform 58.com.
Joyce ZK Lim is The Straits Times’ China correspondent, based in Shenzhen.
In time to come, it plans to expand what chores the robot can do, and make the service available in more cities.
They are part of a new cleaning service launched in China in March, as robot start-ups look beyond gongfu and dancing to make humanoids more useful in the real world.

As China grapples with an ageing workforce and declining birth rates, companies are betting on robots to be housekeepers for the future and bringing them into people’s homes to help them learn the job better.
China is the world’s largest producer and user of humanoid robots, a market which investment bank Barclays estimates could reach US$200 billion worldwide by 2035.
SHENZHEN – I opened my home last week to an unlikely trio: a boxy white robot named Quanta X1 Pro and its two human partners – housekeeper Aunty Tan and a young engineer .
A three-hour house-cleaning costs the same with or without the robot.
The robot’s last chore was to remove the used garbage bag from the trash can.
Then she wiped all the surfaces the robot did not clean.
Homes are notoriously tricky for humanoids to clean as the unpredictable environments are filled with finicky tasks.
Robots that can reliably do most household chores without supervision are, by most measures, at least a decade away, he added.
First the robot straightened two chairs at the dining table, grabbing their legs with its pincer-like hands and pushing them into place.

extraction.body: For now, the 1.6m-tall robot fitted on a wheeled base with two mechanical arms would only perform simple tasks and operate in the living area. SHENZHEN – I opened my home last week to an unlikely trio: a boxy white robot named Quanta X1 Pro and its two human partners – housekeeper Aunty Tan and a young engineer . They are part of a new cleaning service launched in China in March, as robot start-ups look beyond gongfu and dancing to make humanoids more useful in the real world. As China grapples with an ageing workforce and declining birth rates, companies are betting on robots to be housekeepers for the future and bringing them into people’s homes to help them learn the job better. Curious, I signed up for a three-hour cleaning service that costs 149 yuan (S$28), available in Shenzhen and Beijing. The cleaning is mainly still done by human hands, the engineer said as Aunty Tan bustled about the kitchen. For now, the 1.6m-tall robot fitted on a wheeled base with two mechanical arms would only perform simple tasks and operate in my living area. I watched as Quanta began by silently scanning the room to figure out what it could and would do. It works mostly autonomously, I was told, but would need help if it got stumped or stuck. The engineer, who declined to give his name, observed its every move, ready to step in if it hit a snag or broke anything. First the robot straightened two chairs at the dining table, grabbing their legs with its pincer-like hands and pushing them into place. The robot tidied my table tops and removed what it decided was trash – yes to a sweet wrapper and a folded leaflet; no to an empty box of Panadol. But instead of throwing both items together, it made two trips to the bin. I wanted to see if Quanta could wipe the dining table – something not part of its usual repertoire – so I set down a damp cloth and a spray bottle of detergent. The robot made wiping motions with the cloth but ignored the bottle, putting it aside as though in the way. It also left breadcrumbs on the table. Quanta wipes a table but could do a better job. The robot’s last chore was to remove the used garbage bag from the trash can. It did not succeed: the bag was probably too full and got stuck, surmised the engineer, who finished the job himself. He also had to help Quanta into my flat when it got stuck at the raised threshold, twice fixed a wire that came loose on its arm, and adjusted its spotty internet connection. The few things the robot did on its own, it did really slowly. In the time that it moseyed about my living room, Aunty Tan cleaned the rest of the flat. She washed the dirty dishes that the robot could not touch as its hands are not waterproof. She also cleaned the kitchen, scrubbed the toilet, mopped the floor and folded the remaining laundry. Then she wiped all the surfaces the robot did not clean. Asked what she thought of her humanoid partner, Aunty Tan was unimpressed. “Humans are still better at cleaning,” she said. “Look at the robot, what did it really do?” Homes are notoriously tricky for humanoids to clean as the unpredictable environments are filled with finicky tasks. The industry also lacks data to train them to be smarter faster. Many firms are training humanoids to do chores like fold clothes and tidy tables in data factories simulating home environments. But X Square Robot, the Shenzhen-based creator of Quanta, is going further with its home cleaning service, a tie-up with life services platform 58.com. To encourage people to open up their homes, the company offers Quanta’s services basically for free. A three-hour house-cleaning costs the same with or without the robot. Earlier on, the robot-inclusive version had even sold for half price to attract sign-ups. A fleet of robots has now worked in nearly 200 homes so far, the firm said. In time to come, it plans to expand what chores the robot can do, and make the service available in more cities. China is the world’s largest producer and user of humanoid robots, a market which investment bank Barclays estimates could reach US$200 billion worldwide by 2035. The country is gunning to deploy them in real-life settings ranging from factory floors to convenience stores, and now living rooms. In the city of Wuhan, Chinese firm GigaAI announced in May upcoming trials of its household humanoid in homes. Residents can apply to have a robot work for free in their homes next year, with priority given to families with old people, children or pets. Over in the United States, robots are also inching into homes. People can pay US$20,000 (S$25,600) to pre-order a household humanoid from start-up 1X Technologies, which is expected to ship this year. The company is upfront about collecting data from people’s homes. Firms are racing to rack up real-world training data as that is a big bottleneck for embodied AI at the moment, said Georg Stieler, head of robotics and automation at Stieler Technology & Market Advisory, a consultancy. Even as the sector rides a funding boom, companies recognise that their technology must improve quickly, “otherwise investors might become sceptical ”, he said. Robots that can reliably do most household chores without supervision are, by most measures, at least a decade away, he added. But in the interim, firms will jostle to put out robots that can do more and do better – with humans like Aunty Tan filling in the gap. The housekeeper did not rule out that the slow-moving humanoid might one day give her a run for her money. In 10 years, she reckoned, “this could all be different”. Joyce ZK Lim is The Straits Times’ China correspondent, based in Shenzhen.

passages: A lawsuit filed by former Ethereum Foundation (EF) Protocol Support lead Kayleen Fulton against Stiftung Ethereum, Vitalik Buterin, and others alleges she was fired after disclosing a cancer diagnosis and organizing opposition to a “suicide pledge.”
Furthermore, the foundation chose to record it permanently on the Ethereum blockchain, with the suicide pledge intact.
Fulton claims that 79 employees voted to remove that section, with one employee citing “a colleague lost to suicide the year before.”
In February of this year, the foundation distributed a draft of its new mandate to employees.
The complaint also alleges that EF Co-Executive Director Bastian Aue insisted that every employee must commit to the mandate or the foundation would assume they had resigned.
