extraction.body: On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years. The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation , a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum , a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds. And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge. Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide. When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge. Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings. Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.” Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.” An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit. Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide. “I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.” Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version. The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit. When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit. After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.” 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Dial 988 for national hotline. It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.” In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit. Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit. “If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair. The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated. Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies. passages: On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.

The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation , a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum , a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.

Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.
And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.

Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.

Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.

Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”

passages: Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow on Thursday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran gather pace, with Tehran seeking Moscow’s support on regional security and post-war arrangements.During the meeting, Khamenei aide Rezaei also handed Putin a letter from Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Iranian state broadcaster Press TV reported, according to Al Jazeera.The meeting came at a time when US President Donald Trump is facing a major political setback after Republicans lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections.

Last month, Putin told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia was prepared to “do everything” it could to support efforts towards that goal, Russian news agencies reported.The Kremlin discussions also covered plans for a gas pipeline linking Russia and Iran.

The proposed project is aimed at helping address Iran’s gas shortages while allowing Moscow to supply gas to countries neighbouring Iran.Rezaei further briefed Putin on a meeting held in Tehran in late October involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

He said the Moscow visit had been planned nearly a month earlier but was postponed due to “daily discussions about the military situation in the region”.He did not disclose the contents of the letter.In a written statement on Wednesday, Khamenei said there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US.

As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said.Rezaei said Putin had reiterated Moscow’s readiness to help bring the conflict to an end.

extraction.body: Putin meets Iran’s top security official to discuss regional security and receives a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow to discuss regional security as diplomatic efforts gather pace to end the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. During the meeting on Thursday, Rezaei also delivered a letter to Putin from Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to the Iranian state broadcaster Press TV. Speaking after the meeting, Rezaei said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US’s “aggression” against Iran. “Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” he said. Other topics, he said, included plans to deepen energy cooperation, including building gas pipelines from Russia to Iran. Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Khamenei had wanted him to deliver the message to Putin as soon as possible. The trip to Moscow had been planned nearly a month earlier, he said, but was postponed due to “daily discussions about the military situation in the region”. Khamenei said in a written statement on Wednesday that there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US. He also called for an “ever stronger” Iran to reach a “point of absolute deterrence”. Rezaei’s meeting with Putin came as Qatar steps up diplomatic efforts to end the war on Iran amid fears the US could renew attacks following its midterm elections. In Tuesday’s vote, US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate amid widespread anger over rising prices that many blame on the war on Iran. Efforts to end the conflict have centred on the future status of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a US blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions against Iran, and a resumption of negotiations over the country’s nuclear programme. Rezaei said on Thursday that Tehran would not hold talks with the US on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz until Washington meets its seven demands . “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said. According to Rezaei, Putin reiterated that Russia is ready to provide support to end the war. Last month, Putin told Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia was prepared to “ do everything ” it could towards that end, Russian news agencies reported. Rezaei said the discussion at the Kremlin also focused on the construction of a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran, aimed at addressing Iran’s gas shortages and enabling Russia to sell its gas to countries neighbouring Iran. He added that he had briefed Putin on a meeting held in Tehran in late October among Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, and that the Russian leader had welcomed it. “Like our Chinese friends, we believe that there should be regional arrangements and that foreign countries should not interfere in the security of the region,” he said. The Kremlin did not immediately release its own account of the meeting, which took place in the Senate Palace, according to Russia’s TASS news agency. Separately, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with his counterparts in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Turkiye and Jordan. His calls focused on regional developments and ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote peace, Iranian state media reported. Russia and Iran, both under heavy Western sanctions, have strengthened their diplomatic and military ties in recent years. In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture and education. The treaty took effect that October, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it does not include a mutual defence clause. On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Iran had bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets and expected to receive them after the war ends. The planes were originally supposed to arrive before the fighting began, he told the Iranian news site Tabnak, and the necessary preparations and pilot training were complete.

He also called for an “ever stronger” Iran to reach a “point of absolute deterrence”. Rezaei’s meeting with Putin came as Qatar steps up diplomatic efforts to end the war on Iran amid fears the US could renew attacks following its midterm elections. In Tuesday’s vote, US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate amid widespread anger over rising prices that many blame on the war on Iran. Efforts to end the conflict have centred on the future status of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a US blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions against Iran, and a resumption of negotiations over the country’s nuclear programme. Rezaei said on Thursday that Tehran would not hold talks with the US on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz until Washington meets its seven demands . “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said. Last month, Putin told Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia was prepared to “ do everything ” it could towards that end, Russian news agencies reported. The Kremlin did not immediately release its own account of the meeting, which took place in the Senate Palace, according to Russia’s TASS news agency. Separately, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with his counterparts in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Turkiye and Jordan. His calls focused on regional developments and ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote peace, Iranian state media reported. In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture and education. extraction.body: An elected head of state’s term could stretch across three electoral cycles, potentially nine years, for the Australian Parliament (Brendon Thorne/Bloomberg via Getty Images) In the recently proposed model, a mandate from the head of state would override the prime minister. That’s a problem. Australian republicanism poses difficult foreign policy questions The national dignity conferred by true independence warrants the best possible constitutional model for an Australian republic. But one of the main stumbling blocks to Australia moving from constitutional monarchy is the uncertainty around what model should replace it. While serious discussion of alternatives is welcome, it’s disappointing that the model recently proposed by the Australian Republic Movement (ARM), the leading voice for constitutional change in Australia, is premised more on polling than rigorous considerations of national governance, not least in foreign policy and national security. The “Australian Choice Model” proposes a popularly elected head of state, serving up to two 5-year terms, with candidates nominated by Australian parliaments. Most importantly, the head of state’s substantive powers would largely mirror those of the Governor-General. As former prime minister Paul Keating and constitutional law expert Professor Anne Twomey have pointed out, the essential problem with the ARM’s proposed model is that it would create “ rival power centres ”. As Twomey says , “[i]f you have an elected head of state the biggest concern is they have a mandate from the people and that mandate from a directly elected head of state would override the mandate of the prime minister who is not directly elected by the people.” Ambiguity or, worse, outright discrepancy between prime minister and head of state tempts exploitation by adversaries and diminishes trust from allies and friends. The reason the current model functions well enough is precisely because the Governor-General’s mandate is the sovereign’s appointment on the advice of the Prime Minister. While a shift to a republic is an important change for Australia’s identity and full independence, a minimum of substantive change is preferrable to maintain stability and certainty at the highest levels of governance. The ARM’s model, however, represents a radical change: an Australian head of state with a unique mandate, one that is especially relevant to the most truly “national” areas of policy, such as foreign affairs and national security. It is vital that the Australian Government has unity of intent and action in security and foreign relations. Ambiguity or, worse, outright discrepancy between prime minister and head of state tempts exploitation by adversaries and diminishes trust from allies and friends. The problem starts in the electoral process. Any candidate for head of state would develop a platform to differentiate themselves. Any sensible candidate would campaign on matters of national importance – so defence and foreign affairs will be front and centre. If a sitting government is unpopular in one of these areas, a candidate for head of state may campaign based on frustrating their policies. Moreover, having a national popular vote for head of state is likely to deter the kind of eminent apolitical figures Australians have enjoyed as Governor-General and instead attract partisan figures accustomed to a combative process. A popular mandate to do nothing at all is an oxymoron. An elected head of state will have an agenda and the will to implement it. Once elected, the head of state’s term would stretch across at least two, but potentially three, electoral cycles (currently three years) for the Australian Parliament. In this time, the national mandate of the head of state would remain, but the party of government and their policies could change multiple times. The ARM’s model effectively retains the current position entrenched by section 63 of the Constitution that the head of state must act upon the advice of ministers and cabinet. The issue, however, is that while this would be strictly true for matters of law or government action, it is unlikely to constrain how a head of state uses their platform. The bully pulpit is a powerful tool for a popularly elected head of state: a lever that could be used to influence, and even change, policy through public sentiment. Moreover, how an elected head of state would represent Australia to the world is quite unclear. Would they faithfully enact the government’s foreign policy, or forge their own diplomatic agenda? A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government. It’s not hard to imagine a clash between head of state and prime minister. A progressive head of state elected on a platform of vigorously advancing human rights would likely conflcit with the kind of hard-line immigration policies the current Government holds. Similarly, a head of state intent on promoting Australian liberal values could undermine the pragmatic diplomacy needed with less like-minded countries. And, of course, on an issue as high stakes as China policy, divergent views are almost inevitable. A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government. The most dangerous implication of the ARM’s model, however, is the head of state’s power as commander-in-chief. Currently, under section 68 of the Constitution, “[t]he command in chief of the naval and military forces of the Commonwealth is vested in the Governor-General as the Queen's representative.” While the ARM’s model does not state how section 68 might change, it’s fair to assume that a head of state would exercise this power based on ministerial advice. But the issue is more complex. Ambiguity persists around how section 68 can be exercised currently. Moreover, section 68 is supplemented by the Crown’s co-existing prerogative power of war . Precisely how these powers would operate in a republic must be made clear. A head of state acting independently with armed force or countermanding the cabinet’s instructions would be a fraught situation. The irony of the ARM’s proposal is that it highlights the upsides of constitutional monarchy. Australia would be better served by going for a minimum-change model where, for instance, the head of state is nominated by the prime minister and elected by a two-thirds majority of a joint-sitting of parliament. In something as fundamental as constitutional governance, there’s no room for a sub-optimal model. passages: Over the past week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attended the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda.

On 3 November, Albanese addressed the opening of the CHOGM Joint Forums , highlighting the importance of international cooperation on trade, climate change, artificial intelligence and democratic resilience.
He emphasised the need to support smaller states, particularly in the Pacific and Caribbean, in responding to economic and climate challenges.
Albanese also reaffirmed Australia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2029–30.
The initiative supports the international goal of protecting 30 per cent of the world’s land and oceans by 2030.

On 4 November, Australia and the United Kingdom released a joint statement committing to stronger cooperation in addressing online violence and threats against parliamentarians across the Commonwealth.
The statement highlighted the disproportionate impact of online harassment and gender-based threats on women in politics and the risks these pose to democratic participation.

Both governments committed to working with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association and Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians to develop practical solutions, including through technology and expertise sharing.
The first Commonwealth forum addressing these challenges will be held in 2027.

On 31 October, Foreign Minister Penny Wong joined her counterparts from the United States, India and Japan for the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific, with discussions focusing on economic security, critical minerals, maritime security and emerging technologies. The Quad welcomed progress in diversifying critical mineral supply chains, including through recycling initiatives, and outlined plans to provide more than US$85 million in technical and financial assistance to expand access to trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific. Ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea and announced plans for the first Quad Business Leaders’ Forum. Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific, with discussions focusing on economic security, critical minerals, maritime security and emerging technologies. The Quad welcomed progress in diversifying critical mineral supply chains, including through recycling initiatives, and outlined plans to provide more than US$85 million in technical and financial assistance to expand access to trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific. Ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea and announced plans for the first Quad Business Leaders’ Forum.

extraction.body: An elected head of state’s term could stretch across three electoral cycles, potentially nine years, for the Australian Parliament (Brendon Thorne/Bloomberg via Getty Images) In the recently proposed model, a mandate from the head of state would override the prime minister. That’s a problem. Australian republicanism poses difficult foreign policy questions The national dignity conferred by true independence warrants the best possible constitutional model for an Australian republic. But one of the main stumbling blocks to Australia moving from constitutional monarchy is the uncertainty around what model should replace it. While serious discussion of alternatives is welcome, it’s disappointing that the model recently proposed by the Australian Republic Movement (ARM), the leading voice for constitutional change in Australia, is premised more on polling than rigorous considerations of national governance, not least in foreign policy and national security. The “Australian Choice Model” proposes a popularly elected head of state, serving up to two 5-year terms, with candidates nominated by Australian parliaments. Most importantly, the head of state’s substantive powers would largely mirror those of the Governor-General. As former prime minister Paul Keating and constitutional law expert Professor Anne Twomey have pointed out, the essential problem with the ARM’s proposed model is that it would create “ rival power centres ”. As Twomey says , “[i]f you have an elected head of state the biggest concern is they have a mandate from the people and that mandate from a directly elected head of state would override the mandate of the prime minister who is not directly elected by the people.” Ambiguity or, worse, outright discrepancy between prime minister and head of state tempts exploitation by adversaries and diminishes trust from allies and friends. The reason the current model functions well enough is precisely because the Governor-General’s mandate is the sovereign’s appointment on the advice of the Prime Minister. While a shift to a republic is an important change for Australia’s identity and full independence, a minimum of substantive change is preferrable to maintain stability and certainty at the highest levels of governance. The ARM’s model, however, represents a radical change: an Australian head of state with a unique mandate, one that is especially relevant to the most truly “national” areas of policy, such as foreign affairs and national security. It is vital that the Australian Government has unity of intent and action in security and foreign relations. Ambiguity or, worse, outright discrepancy between prime minister and head of state tempts exploitation by adversaries and diminishes trust from allies and friends. The problem starts in the electoral process. Any candidate for head of state would develop a platform to differentiate themselves. Any sensible candidate would campaign on matters of national importance – so defence and foreign affairs will be front and centre. If a sitting government is unpopular in one of these areas, a candidate for head of state may campaign based on frustrating their policies. Moreover, having a national popular vote for head of state is likely to deter the kind of eminent apolitical figures Australians have enjoyed as Governor-General and instead attract partisan figures accustomed to a combative process. A popular mandate to do nothing at all is an oxymoron. An elected head of state will have an agenda and the will to implement it. Once elected, the head of state’s term would stretch across at least two, but potentially three, electoral cycles (currently three years) for the Australian Parliament. In this time, the national mandate of the head of state would remain, but the party of government and their policies could change multiple times. The ARM’s model effectively retains the current position entrenched by section 63 of the Constitution that the head of state must act upon the advice of ministers and cabinet. The issue, however, is that while this would be strictly true for matters of law or government action, it is unlikely to constrain how a head of state uses their platform. The bully pulpit is a powerful tool for a popularly elected head of state: a lever that could be used to influence, and even change, policy through public sentiment. Moreover, how an elected head of state would represent Australia to the world is quite unclear. Would they faithfully enact the government’s foreign policy, or forge their own diplomatic agenda? A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government. It’s not hard to imagine a clash between head of state and prime minister. A progressive head of state elected on a platform of vigorously advancing human rights would likely conflcit with the kind of hard-line immigration policies the current Government holds. Similarly, a head of state intent on promoting Australian liberal values could undermine the pragmatic diplomacy needed with less like-minded countries. And, of course, on an issue as high stakes as China policy, divergent views are almost inevitable. A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government. The most dangerous implication of the ARM’s model, however, is the head of state’s power as commander-in-chief. Currently, under section 68 of the Constitution, “[t]he command in chief of the naval and military forces of the Commonwealth is vested in the Governor-General as the Queen's representative.” While the ARM’s model does not state how section 68 might change, it’s fair to assume that a head of state would exercise this power based on ministerial advice. But the issue is more complex. Ambiguity persists around how section 68 can be exercised currently. Moreover, section 68 is supplemented by the Crown’s co-existing prerogative power of war . Precisely how these powers would operate in a republic must be made clear. A head of state acting independently with armed force or countermanding the cabinet’s instructions would be a fraught situation. The irony of the ARM’s proposal is that it highlights the upsides of constitutional monarchy. Australia would be better served by going for a minimum-change model where, for instance, the head of state is nominated by the prime minister and elected by a two-thirds majority of a joint-sitting of parliament. In something as fundamental as constitutional governance, there’s no room for a sub-optimal model. Moreover, how an elected head of state would represent Australia to the world is quite unclear. Would they faithfully enact the government’s foreign policy, or forge their own diplomatic agenda?
A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government.

It’s not hard to imagine a clash between head of state and prime minister. A progressive head of state elected on a platform of vigorously advancing human rights would likely conflcit with the kind of hard-line immigration policies the current Government holds. Similarly, a head of state intent on promoting Australian liberal values could undermine the pragmatic diplomacy needed with less like-minded countries. And, of course, on an issue as high stakes as China policy, divergent views are almost inevitable. A head of state nearing the end of their term but seeking a legacy may feel particularly empowered to act at odds with the government.

The most dangerous implication of the ARM’s model, however, is the head of state’s power as commander-in-chief. Currently, under section 68 of the Constitution, “[t]he command in chief of the naval and military forces of the Commonwealth is vested in the Governor-General as the Queen's representative.” While the ARM’s model does not state how section 68 might change, it’s fair to assume that a head of state would exercise this power based on ministerial advice. But the issue is more complex. Ambiguity persists around how section 68 can be exercised currently. Moreover, section 68 is supplemented by the Crown’s co-existing prerogative power of war . Precisely how these powers would operate in a republic must be made clear. A head of state acting independently with armed force or countermanding the cabinet’s instructions would be a fraught situation.

The irony of the ARM’s proposal is that it highlights the upsides of constitutional monarchy. Australia would be better served by going for a minimum-change model where, for instance, the head of state is nominated by the prime minister and elected by a two-thirds majority of a joint-sitting of parliament. In something as fundamental as constitutional governance, there’s no room for a sub-optimal model.
Sarah Thompson , Dominic de Moura McCarthy , Sharon Bala Woruba

He emphasised the need to support smaller states, particularly in the Pacific and Caribbean, in responding to economic and climate challenges.
Albanese also reaffirmed Australia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2029–30.
The initiative supports the international goal of protecting 30 per cent of the world’s land and oceans by 2030.

extraction.body: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts The Week in Australian Foreign Affairs 6 November: This Week in Australian Foreign Affairs This week in Australian foreign affairs: Australia advanced economic and maritime security cooperation through the Quad, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attended the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Australia and the United Kingdom committed to addressing online violence against parliamentarians, new sanctions were imposed on Sudanese military leaders, and more. On 31 October, Foreign Minister Penny Wong joined her counterparts from the United States, India and Japan for the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific, with discussions focusing on economic security, critical minerals, maritime security and emerging technologies. The Quad welcomed progress in diversifying critical mineral supply chains, including through recycling initiatives, and outlined plans to provide more than US$85 million in technical and financial assistance to expand access to trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific. Ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea and announced plans for the first Quad Business Leaders’ Forum. Over the past week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attended the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda. On 3 November, Albanese addressed the opening of the CHOGM Joint Forums , highlighting the importance of international cooperation on trade, climate change, artificial intelligence and democratic resilience. He emphasised the need to support smaller states, particularly in the Pacific and Caribbean, in responding to economic and climate challenges. Albanese also reaffirmed Australia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2029–30. During CHOGM, Albanese held bilateral discussions with United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Discussions with Burnham included progress on AUKUS, particularly the development of nuclear-powered submarines in Australia and the United Kingdom. Albanese also discussed critical minerals, defence cooperation and trade diversification with Carney, including ongoing negotiations towards an Australia–European Union Free Trade Agreement. Also on 3 November, Albanese attended the Commonwealth Nature Initiative side event , which brought together governments, businesses and philanthropic organisations to encourage investment in biodiversity conservation. The initiative supports the international goal of protecting 30 per cent of the world’s land and oceans by 2030. Albanese highlighted Australia’s Sustainable Ocean Plan, its ratification of the High Seas Biodiversity Treaty and ongoing cooperation with Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Timor-Leste to address marine debris. He also reaffirmed Australia’s commitment to supporting Pacific island countries facing the impacts of climate change. On 4 November, Australia and the United Kingdom released a joint statement committing to stronger cooperation in addressing online violence and threats against parliamentarians across the Commonwealth. The statement highlighted the disproportionate impact of online harassment and gender-based threats on women in politics and the risks these pose to democratic participation. Both governments committed to working with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association and Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians to develop practical solutions, including through technology and expertise sharing. The first Commonwealth forum addressing these challenges will be held in 2027. The following day, Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced new targeted human rights sanctions and travel bans against four Sudanese individuals, alongside financial sanctions on one entity, in response to serious human rights violations during Sudan’s ongoing civil war. Those sanctioned include Sudanese Armed Forces leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Rapid Support Forces commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. Since the conflict began in April 2023, more than 14 million people have been displaced, while almost 34 million require humanitarian assistance. Australia has provided over $67 million in humanitarian assistance and called for an immediate and permanent ceasefire, the protection of civilians and unrestricted humanitarian access. "We saw continued strong momentum in our fiscal second quarter, delivering our seventh consecutive quarter of sequential sales growth. Sales were $277 million, representing a 29% increase year-over-year. GAAP earnings per share quadrupled from $0.03 per share in the fiscal second quarter of 2026 to $0.12. Non-GAAP EPS grew to $0.26, doubling over the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Broad year-over-year sales growth in Automotive and Industrial end markets drove this strong performance, led by data center, which established a new record," said Mike Doogue, President and CEO of Allegro. "Our forward demand signals strengthened significantly this quarter. We delivered our highest quarterly design-win performance since our 2020 IPO—up nearly 40% year-over-year—and bookings increased for the eighth consecutive quarter. With record design wins, a robust backlog, and expanding content across our target Automotive and Industrial markets, the leading indicators across our business give us high confidence in our path to exceed our target model of mid-teens annual sales growth." "During the quarter, we also continued to execute on our strategic priorities of expanding profitability and generating strong cash flow," said Derek D'Antilio, Executive Vice President and CFO of Allegro. extraction.body: CHANDLER, Ariz., Nov. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- (NASDAQ: MCHP) - Microchip Technology Incorporated, a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today reported results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. "Our September quarter net sales were above the high end of our guidance, increasing 42.2% year over year and 9.2% sequentially to $1.622 billion," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip’s President and Chief Executive Officer. "The momentum from the start of fiscal 2027 continued in the September quarter, with broad-based growth across our end markets, driven by industrial and data center applications. Our growth is increasingly supported by new design wins and product innovations, which we believe positions us well for the opportunities ahead." Mr. Sanghi added, “Bookings remained robust, with book-to-bill well above one, consistent with recent quarters. We are winning new designs across our end markets, including data center, where our PCIe Gen6 switch and retimer design wins have grown to 24 to date, up from 12 at the end of the June quarter. We also broadened our portfolio, with a steady cadence of product and technology introductions across data center, aerospace and defense, automotive and industrial applications, which expands the foundation for future design wins." Eric Bjornholt, Microchip's Corporate Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, said, "Our September quarter results reflect ongoing operational improvements, with non-GAAP operating expenses growing well below net sales and supporting higher profitability. We believe our existing manufacturing footprint enables us to grow with modest incremental capital investment, and we remain focused on strengthening our balance sheet while making targeted investments that accelerate our product roadmap.” Mr. Sanghi concluded, “As we enter the December quarter, we are experiencing some normal seasonal factors in our business. Normal seasonality is for our revenue to be down sequentially 3% to 5% in the December quarter. We expect net sales for the December quarter to be between down 3% and up 1% sequentially, with a midpoint of down 1%. The midpoint of our December quarter guidance represents year-over-year growth of approximately 35.4%. Our guidance of down 1% at the midpoint needs to be considered with the fact that we had about $53 million of infrequent revenue items in the September quarter which do not repeat in the December quarter. Taking this into consideration, the midpoint of our guidance for the December quarter represents guidance that is 5% to 7% better than normal seasonality. Lead times are lengthening across our supply chain, and we are working to expand capacity and secure additional wafer allocation. We expect non-GAAP gross margin to be between 64% and 65% and GAAP gross margin to be between 62.9% and 63.9%. Together, data center, aerospace and defense, industrials, robotics, automotive and the intelligent edge are the secular trends we see driving growth over the long-term.” The following table summarizes Microchip's reported results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 was $373.6 million, or $0.68 per diluted share, up from GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders of $13.9 million, or $0.03 per diluted share, in the prior year's second fiscal quarter. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, GAAP results were adversely impacted by amortization of acquired intangible assets associated with our previous acquisitions. Non-GAAP net income for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 was $559.2 million, or $0.97 per diluted share, up from non-GAAP net income of $199.1 million, or $0.35 per diluted share, in the prior year's second fiscal quarter. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, our non-GAAP results exclude the effect of share-based compensation, restructuring charges, expenses related to our acquisition activities (including intangible asset amortization, severance, other restructuring costs, and legal and other general and administrative expenses including legal fees and expenses for litigation related to our Microsemi acquisition), professional services associated with certain legal matters, (gain) loss on available-for-sale investments, and dividends on our Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, our non-GAAP income tax expense is presented based on projected cash taxes for the applicable fiscal year, excluding transition tax payments under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. A reconciliation of our non-GAAP and GAAP results is included in this press release. Microchip announced today that its Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend on its common stock of 45.5 cents per share, which is payable on December 8, 2026 to stockholders of record on November 23, 2026. Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures: Our non-GAAP adjustments, where applicable, include the effect of share-based compensation, restructuring charges, expenses related to our acquisition activities (including intangible asset amortization, severance, other restructuring costs, and legal and other general and administrative expenses including legal fees and expenses for litigation related to our Microsemi acquisition), professional services associated with certain legal matters, (gain) loss on available-for-sale investments, and dividends on our Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, our non-GAAP income tax expense is presented based on projected cash taxes for the fiscal year, excluding transition tax payments under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.

We are required to estimate the cost of certain forms of share-based compensation, including restricted stock units and our employee stock purchase plan, and to record a commensurate expense in our income statement. Share-based compensation expense is a non-cash expense that varies in amount from period to period and is affected by the price of our stock at the date of grant. The price of our stock is affected by market forces that are difficult to predict and are not within the control of management. Our other non-GAAP adjustments are either non-cash expenses, unusual or infrequent items, or other expenses related to transactions. Management excludes all of these items from its internal operating forecasts and models.

We are using non-GAAP operating expenses in dollars, including non-GAAP research and development expenses and non-GAAP selling, general and administrative expenses, non-GAAP other expense, net, and non-GAAP income tax rate, which exclude the items noted above, as applicable, to permit additional analysis of our performance.

Management believes these non-GAAP measures are useful to investors because they enhance the understanding of our historical financial performance and comparability between periods. Many of our investors have requested that we disclose this non-GAAP information because they believe it is useful in understanding our performance as it excludes non-cash and other charges that many investors feel may obscure our underlying operating results. Management uses non-GAAP measures to manage and assess the profitability of our business and for compensation purposes. We also use our non-GAAP results when developing and monitoring our budgets and spending. Our determination of these non-GAAP measures might

not be the same as similarly titled measures used by other companies, and it should not be construed as a substitute for amounts determined in accordance with GAAP. Generally, gross profit fluctuates over time, driven primarily by the mix of products sold and licensing revenue; variances in manufacturing yields; fixed cost absorption; wafer fab loading levels; costs of wafers from foundries; inventory reserves; pricing pressures in our non-proprietary product lines; and competitive and economic conditions. Operating expenses fluctuate over time, primarily due to net sales and profit levels.

extraction.body: Second Quarter Sales Increased by 29% Year-over-Year to $277 Million Record Industrial & Other and Data Center Sales GAAP EPS Quadrupled and Non-GAAP EPS Doubled Year-over-Year MANCHESTER, N.H., Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Allegro MicroSystems, Inc. ("Allegro" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: ALGM ), a global leader in power and sensing semiconductor solutions for motion control and energy efficient systems, today announced financial results for its second quarter ended September 25, 2026. "We saw continued strong momentum in our fiscal second quarter, delivering our seventh consecutive quarter of sequential sales growth. Sales were $277 million, representing a 29% increase year-over-year. GAAP earnings per share quadrupled from $0.03 per share in the fiscal second quarter of 2026 to $0.12. Non-GAAP EPS grew to $0.26, doubling over the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Broad year-over-year sales growth in Automotive and Industrial end markets drove this strong performance, led by data center, which established a new record," said Mike Doogue, President and CEO of Allegro. "Our forward demand signals strengthened significantly this quarter. We delivered our highest quarterly design-win performance since our 2020 IPO—up nearly 40% year-over-year—and bookings increased for the eighth consecutive quarter. With record design wins, a robust backlog, and expanding content across our target Automotive and Industrial markets, the leading indicators across our business give us high confidence in our path to exceed our target model of mid-teens annual sales growth." "During the quarter, we also continued to execute on our strategic priorities of expanding profitability and generating strong cash flow," said Derek D'Antilio, Executive Vice President and CFO of Allegro. "On September 30, 2026, following the close of the second quarter, we made another $25 million voluntary debt repayment, underscoring the strength of our balance sheet and our confidence in Allegro's anticipated free cash flow generation." For the third quarter of fiscal year 2027 ending December 25, 2026, the Company expects total net sales to be in the range of $278 million to $288 million. At the midpoint of this range, it implies growth in net sales of 23% year-over-year. The Company also estimates the following results on a non-GAAP basis: Gross Margin is expected to be between 51.5% and 52.5%, Diluted Earnings per Share is expected to be between $0.25 and $0.29, with the mid-point of this range implying an 80% year-over-year increase. Allegro has not provided a reconciliation of its third fiscal quarter outlook for non-GAAP Gross Margin, non-GAAP Operating Expenses, and non-GAAP Diluted Earnings per Share because estimates of all of the reconciling items cannot be provided without unreasonable efforts. MANCHESTER, N.H., Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Allegro MicroSystems, Inc. ("Allegro" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: ALGM ), a global leader in power and sensing semiconductor solutions for motion control and energy efficient systems, today announced financial results for its second quarter ended September 25, 2026.

"We saw continued strong momentum in our fiscal second quarter, delivering our seventh consecutive quarter of sequential sales growth. Sales were $277 million, representing a 29% increase year-over-year. GAAP earnings per share quadrupled from $0.03 per share in the fiscal second quarter of 2026 to $0.12. Non-GAAP EPS grew to $0.26, doubling over the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Broad year-over-year sales growth in Automotive and Industrial end markets drove this strong performance, led by data center, which established a new record," said Mike Doogue, President and CEO of Allegro. "Our forward demand signals strengthened significantly this quarter. We delivered our highest quarterly design-win performance since our 2020 IPO—up nearly 40% year-over-year—and bookings increased for the eighth consecutive quarter. With record design wins, a robust backlog, and expanding content across our target Automotive and Industrial markets, the leading indicators across our business give us high confidence in our path to exceed our target model of mid-teens annual sales growth."

"During the quarter, we also continued to execute on our strategic priorities of expanding profitability and generating strong cash flow," said Derek D'Antilio, Executive Vice President and CFO of Allegro. "On September 30, 2026, following the close of the second quarter, we made another $25 million voluntary debt repayment, underscoring the strength of our balance sheet and our confidence in Allegro's anticipated free cash flow generation."

extraction.body: CHANDLER, Ariz., Nov. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- (NASDAQ: MCHP) - Microchip Technology Incorporated, a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today reported results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. "Our September quarter net sales were above the high end of our guidance, increasing 42.2% year over year and 9.2% sequentially to $1.622 billion," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip’s President and Chief Executive Officer. "The momentum from the start of fiscal 2027 continued in the September quarter, with broad-based growth across our end markets, driven by industrial and data center applications. Our growth is increasingly supported by new design wins and product innovations, which we believe positions us well for the opportunities ahead." Mr. Sanghi added, “Bookings remained robust, with book-to-bill well above one, consistent with recent quarters. We are winning new designs across our end markets, including data center, where our PCIe Gen6 switch and retimer design wins have grown to 24 to date, up from 12 at the end of the June quarter. We also broadened our portfolio, with a steady cadence of product and technology introductions across data center, aerospace and defense, automotive and industrial applications, which expands the foundation for future design wins." Eric Bjornholt, Microchip's Corporate Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, said, "Our September quarter results reflect ongoing operational improvements, with non-GAAP operating expenses growing well below net sales and supporting higher profitability. We believe our existing manufacturing footprint enables us to grow with modest incremental capital investment, and we remain focused on strengthening our balance sheet while making targeted investments that accelerate our product roadmap.” Mr. Sanghi concluded, “As we enter the December quarter, we are experiencing some normal seasonal factors in our business. Normal seasonality is for our revenue to be down sequentially 3% to 5% in the December quarter. We expect net sales for the December quarter to be between down 3% and up 1% sequentially, with a midpoint of down 1%. The midpoint of our December quarter guidance represents year-over-year growth of approximately 35.4%. Our guidance of down 1% at the midpoint needs to be considered with the fact that we had about $53 million of infrequent revenue items in the September quarter which do not repeat in the December quarter. Taking this into consideration, the midpoint of our guidance for the December quarter represents guidance that is 5% to 7% better than normal seasonality. Lead times are lengthening across our supply chain, and we are working to expand capacity and secure additional wafer allocation. We expect non-GAAP gross margin to be between 64% and 65% and GAAP gross margin to be between 62.9% and 63.9%. Together, data center, aerospace and defense, industrials, robotics, automotive and the intelligent edge are the secular trends we see driving growth over the long-term.” The following table summarizes Microchip's reported results for the three months ended September 30, 2026. passages: CHANDLER, Ariz., Nov. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- (NASDAQ: MCHP) - Microchip Technology Incorporated, a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today reported results for the three months ended September 30, 2026.

"Our September quarter net sales were above the high end of our guidance, increasing 42.2% year over year and 9.2% sequentially to $1.622 billion," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip’s President and Chief Executive Officer. "The momentum from the start of fiscal 2027 continued in the September quarter, with broad-based growth across our end markets, driven by industrial and data center applications. Our growth is increasingly supported by new design wins and product innovations, which we believe positions us well for the opportunities ahead."

Mr. Sanghi added, “Bookings remained robust, with book-to-bill well above one, consistent with recent quarters. We are winning new designs across our end markets, including data center, where our PCIe Gen6 switch and retimer design wins have grown to 24 to date, up from 12 at the end of the June quarter. We also broadened our portfolio, with a steady cadence of product and technology introductions across data center, aerospace and defense, automotive and industrial applications, which expands the foundation for future design wins."

Eric Bjornholt, Microchip's Corporate Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, said, "Our September quarter results reflect ongoing operational improvements, with non-GAAP operating expenses growing well below net sales and supporting higher profitability. We believe our existing manufacturing footprint enables us to grow with modest incremental capital investment, and we remain focused on strengthening our balance sheet while making targeted investments that accelerate our product roadmap.”

Mr. Sanghi concluded, “As we enter the December quarter, we are experiencing some normal seasonal factors in our business. Normal seasonality is for our revenue to be down sequentially 3% to 5% in the December quarter. We expect net sales for the December quarter to be between down 3% and up 1% sequentially, with a midpoint of down 1%. The midpoint of our December quarter guidance represents year-over-year growth of approximately 35.4%. Our guidance of down 1% at the midpoint needs to be considered with the fact that we had about $53 million of infrequent revenue items in the September quarter which do not repeat in the December quarter. Taking this into consideration, the midpoint of our guidance for the December quarter represents guidance that is 5% to 7% better than normal seasonality. Lead times are lengthening across our supply chain, and we are working to expand capacity and secure additional wafer allocation. We expect non-GAAP gross margin to be between 64% and 65% and GAAP gross margin to be between 62.9% and 63.9%. Together, data center, aerospace and defense, industrials, robotics, automotive and the intelligent edge are the secular trends we see driving growth over the long-term.”

Net sales for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 were $1.622 billion, up 42.2% from net sales of $1.140 billion in the prior year's second fiscal quarter.

GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 was $373.6 million, or $0.68 per diluted share, up from GAAP net income attributable to common stockholders of $13.9 million, or $0.03 per diluted share, in the prior year's second fiscal quarter. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, GAAP results were adversely impacted by amortization of acquired intangible assets associated with our previous acquisitions.

Non-GAAP net income for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 was $559.2 million, or $0.97 per diluted share, up from non-GAAP net income of $199.1 million, or $0.35 per diluted share, in the prior year's second fiscal quarter. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, our non-GAAP results exclude the effect of share-based compensation, restructuring charges, expenses related to our acquisition activities (including intangible asset amortization, severance, other restructuring costs, and legal and other general and administrative expenses including legal fees and expenses for litigation related to our Microsemi acquisition), professional services associated with certain legal matters, (gain) loss on available-for-sale investments, and dividends on our Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock. For the second quarters of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2026, our non-GAAP income tax expense is presented based on projected cash taxes for the applicable fiscal year, excluding transition tax payments under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. A reconciliation of our non-GAAP and GAAP results is included in this press release.

Microchip announced today that its Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend on its common stock of 45.5 cents per share, which is payable on December 8, 2026 to stockholders of record on November 23, 2026. Our Board also declared a quarterly cash dividend on Microchip's 7.50% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock of $18.750 per share (which represents $0.9375 per depositary share) which is payable on December 15, 2026 to stockholders of record on December 1, 2026.

Microchip also announced that, on November 3, 2026, Victor Peng informed our Board of Directors of his decision to step down from the Board due to his time commitments on other matters including serving as Chief Executive Officer of PsiQuantum. The Board thanks Mr. Peng for his service and contributions during his tenure on the Board.
The following statements are based on current expectations. These statements are forward-looking, and actual results may differ materially.

passages: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.
Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.
He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip.
Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.
“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment.
But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational.
Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.
In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips.
They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that.
So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.
The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates.
It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.
Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences.

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.

“What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”
The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs.

In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself.

“Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote.

Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year.
While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027.

The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.

“Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. extraction.body: The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank. U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries. “If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn. The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers. Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters . The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence . The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran ; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit . CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor. In a separate fact sheet , the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries. “If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn. The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers. The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran ; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit . CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
